sens: Building or underground storage where crops and provisions are kept
Place of accumulation and security for essential goods for life
Image of wealth and divine abundance granted to the people
H4200.detail:
1. The granary is the building or space (often underground or adapted) where a family, city, or country stores its harvests of wheat, barley, and other grains after the harvest. It is an essential storage place for surviving the winter and periods of famine. In Psalms 144:13, the psalmist lists the signs of divine blessing: the granaries are full, overflowing with provisions of all kinds.
2. The granary also represents material security and trust: having filled granaries means being able to face the future without fear. It is the image of a stable life, a family provided for and sheltered from need.
3. Biblically, full granaries symbolize God's blessing and generosity toward His people. When the psalm speaks of granaries "overflowing," it celebrates God's work that multiplies harvests and flocks.
H4200.origine: The Hebrew word מָזוּ (mezou) or מָזוֹן (mazon, food) literally means what allows one to live. The root evokes the idea of providing, of nourishing. The term is related to other Hebrew words concerning food and sustenance. It is concrete vocabulary, tied to the agrarian daily life of the people of Israel.
H4200.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 144:13. The context is a psalm of praise where the psalmist enumerates the visible blessings of God: full granaries, countless flocks, productive fields. It is a description of the prosperity of a blessed nation, at a time when wealth was primarily measured in stored harvests and livestock. The granary here is a concrete and tangible sign of God's benevolent intervention.
H4200.portee: For the biblical reader, the full granary reminds us that material provision comes from God and deserves recognition and praise. It is an invitation to see in concrete goods — food, harvest, large family — not mere possessions, but gifts from the One who watches over His people. It also calls for generosity: a filled granary carries a responsibility toward those who lack.

sens: Vertical support of a door or city gate
Vertical support of a temple or sanctuary door
Bar or structural element of a construction
H4201.detail:
1. The word refers to the vertical support on which a door or city gate hinges. At Passover, the blood of the lamb was placed on "the two posts and the lintel" so that the Lord would recognize the houses of the Israelites (Exodus 12:7). Similarly, the divine commandments were to be written "on the doorposts of your house and on your gates" to keep them constantly in mind (Deuteronomy 6:9). Samson forcefully tore down "the two posts" of the gate of Gaza by seizing them (Judges 16:3).
2. The word also applies to the supports of the temple and sanctuary. The door of the sanctuary had its posts, built of precious wood or adorned with intricate carpentry (1 Kings 6:31).
3. More broadly, it designates any vertical element of an architectural structure, such as the beams or supports of a wall or gallery (1 Kings 7:5).
H4201.origine: The Hebrew word מְזוּזָה comes from a root meaning "side" or "lateral position." It is related to other Hebrew words expressing the idea of side or flank. The initial meaning is that of an element that stands laterally, framing an opening. This word has also given its name to the "mezuzah," the small box containing biblical words that Jews affix to the right post of their doors, in direct application of Deuteronomy 6:9.
H4201.emploi: The word מְזוּזָה appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in ritual laws and architectural descriptions. In Exodus 12, it is linked to Passover: it is on the posts that the blood must be placed. Deuteronomy speaks of it figuratively: the divine Word is written there to be visible, reminding us of the importance of the Law. It is also found in narratives (Samson tearing down the posts, Judges 16:3) and in descriptions of the temple and its structures (1 Kings 6 and 7, Ezekiel). The context shows that it designates either the structure itself (load-bearing, which can be torn down) or an element of decoration or delimitation.
H4201.portee: This word reminds us that the Word of God must be visible and memorized. The practice of writing it on the posts of the house expresses a central truth: God's commandments should not remain secret but be displayed in daily life, in plain sight of all. It is an invitation to let faith guide our entire existence, from the threshold of our home to every decision. The post, a stable element that supports the structure, also evokes the solidity provided by the divine Word.

sens: Food and supplies intended to nourish a person or group during a journey or given period
Food supply provided by an authority to its dependents
H4202.detail:
1. The word refers to the food taken or prepared to sustain someone during a journey or absence. It is a collection of provisions: wheat, bread, and other foods. When Jacob sends Benjamin to Egypt, he "provides him with abundant provisions" (2 Chronicles 11:23) to support him far from home.
2. The word is also used for the supplies that a leader or king distributes to those who depend on him. When Joseph sends his father grain, bread, and provisions (Genesis 45:23), he ensures the food he will need during his journey and afterward. It is an act of care and provision.
H4202.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to nourish" or "to eat." It designates all the material means that sustain physical life. The corresponding Aramaic word has the same form and meaning.
H4202.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. It characterizes two situations of provision: first when Joseph, having become powerful in Egypt, sends provisions for the journey to his father (Genesis 45:23); and secondly when a king distributes abundant food to his sons, scattered in the fortified cities of the kingdom, for their well-being (2 Chronicles 11:23). In both cases, it is a generous and thoughtful provision.
H4202.portee: This word reminds us that providing food for others is an act of love and responsibility. Joseph and this king act as protectors, ensuring that those they love will lack nothing. For the believer, this speaks of God's providence that nourishes and supports us.

sens: What is eaten, the substances we consume for nourishment
What sustains life, sustenance
H4203.detail:
1. The word simply refers to food, the substances consumed to live. In Daniel's vision, the great tree bears "abundant" fruits and offers its "food for all" (Daniel 4:12) — it is the concrete idea of a reserve of accessible food.
2. More broadly, it is what allows one to subsist, the maintenance of life. Every living being — beasts and birds — draws from the great tree "its food" (Daniel 4:12), meaning what sustains it.
H4203.origine: The Hebrew word מָזוֹן (mazon) comes from a root meaning "to prepare" or "to provide." It is an Aramaic word used in Daniel's visions. It designates what is prepared, brought, provided to nourish. The classical Hebrew word for food in the Old Testament is אֹכֶל (okhel, literally "what is eaten").
H4203.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible, only in the passage of the vision of the great tree in Daniel 4. It is used to describe the fruits and substance that this fabulous tree produces in abundance. This mythical tree, which symbolizes a powerful king (Nebuchadnezzar), possesses such an abundance of resources that it nourishes all living beings. The use of the Aramaic word here reflects that Daniel is reporting the divine word received in Aramaic, the official language of the Babylonian empire.
H4203.portee: This word reminds us of a simple truth: everything that lives depends on resources that nourish it. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize that God provides for the needs of His creatures. Jesus will later teach that "man shall not live by bread alone" (Matthew 4:4), suggesting that true food is primarily spiritual.

sens: Device or trick intended to capture or bring someone down
Hidden treachery or deceit
Dangerous situation where one does not perceive the peril
H4204.detail: 1. A trap in the concrete sense is a net, a snare, or a hidden device used to catch an animal or a person — something aimed at capturing or bringing down its victim. In Obadiah 1:7, it is the allies of the king of Edom who set traps for him: they used cunning and treachery against the one they claimed to serve. 2. The trap also evokes treachery: to set a trap for someone is to deceive them while feigning friendship, like those friends who ate the bread of Edom but laid snares for him. 3. A trap can also refer to the danger itself — a situation where one finds oneself hindered, blocked, or defeated without having seen it coming. The text specifies that Edom 'did not know it': the trap acts silently, hidden.
H4204.origine: The Hebrew word mâzôr derives from a root expressing the idea of constraint or encirclement. It primarily denotes a net or a snare that tightens and immobilizes. This image of captivity naturally extends to the figurative sense of treachery or a situation where one finds oneself caught off guard.
H4204.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Obadiah 1:7. The context is the prophecy against the Edomites: God announces that the allies of Edom will turn against him, that those he thought were friends will betray and trap him. It is a condemnation of cunning, unfaithfulness, and misplaced trust. The word emphasizes the irony of this downfall: Edom, politically astute and powerful, will be defeated not by direct force but by the treachery of those who shared his bread.
H4204.portee: This word invites the believer to remain vigilant: the traps of enemies, visible or hidden, threaten those who place their trust anywhere but in God. It reminds us that treachery often comes from those we believe to be our friends, and that God sees and judges these unfaithfulnesses. It is also a call not to set traps for others: to act with sincerity and faithfulness towards brothers.

sens: Open injury on the body, caused by violence
Suffering or misfortune of a people, image of spiritual destruction
H4205.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes a concrete injury, a tear in the skin that bleeds and becomes infected. In Jeremiah 30:13, it speaks of 'binding up the wound', meaning to dress an injury to stop the bleeding and promote healing. 2. The Bible uses this image to speak of the sufferings of the people of Israel or Judah: their misfortune is like a wound that does not heal. In Hosea 5:13, Ephraim and Judah have 'wounds', meaning national injuries, calamities that neither the king of Assyria nor any earthly remedy can heal — only God could heal them.
H4205.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the action of oozing, flowing: a wound is an injury that weeps, that bleeds. The image of a wound to describe collective suffering is common in the prophets: it sensitizes the ear to how the people feel their abandonment or punishment.
H4205.emploi: The word appears twice in the Old Testament, both times in the prophets Jeremiah and Hosea, during a time of national crisis (Assyrian and Babylonian invasions). Jeremiah 30:13 speaks of binding or dressing a wound, in medical language. Hosea 5:13 uses the word in the plural to evoke the multiple wounds of the kingdom — an image of deep distress. In both cases, it is less about physical injuries than about political and spiritual misfortune: the people suffer, they seek a remedy from the powers of the world, and only the healing that God can bring would truly change their situation.
H4205.portee: This word reminds us that sin and unfaithfulness leave wounds: they do not heal on their own, they only heal if a true remedy is applied. For the believer, it is an image of how only God can heal the deepest wounds — not human remedies, not fleeing to the powers of the world.

sens: Strip of fabric that surrounds the waist to hold clothing
That which encircles or compresses
That which weighs like a burden or constraint
H4206A.detail: 1. The belt in the literal sense is a strip of cloth or leather that one wraps around the waist to hold clothing (like pants or a tunic) or to hang a sword. In Psalms 109:19, the belt is mentioned as a garment worn constantly, symbolizing one's condition or status. 2. Figuratively, the word denotes anything that encircles or compresses, recalling the physical sensation of a belt that is too tight. It is a feeling of oppression or imprisonment. 3. By extension, it evokes a yoke, that is, a hindrance, a weight, or a burden imposed from the outside. In Isaiah 23:10, the word designates the yoke of economic or political servitude that the city of Tyre endures, whose daughter (the people) is urged to free herself by traveling freely through her land.
H4206A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning 'to tighten' or 'to surround'. The belt is the object that encircles the body, hence its name. This image of constriction naturally extends into the figurative senses of oppression and burden. The word appears in its nominal form (with a slight vocalic variation in מְזִיחַ) to specifically denote this clothing accessory.
H4206A.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 109:19, it describes an ordinary garment, a belt that someone always wears. In Isaiah 23:10, the context is a prophecy against Tyre, where the word takes on a figurative nuance and designates a yoke, an oppression that the people must shake off. These two uses show the transition from the concrete sense (clothing item) to the abstract sense (oppressive burden).
H4206A.portee: This word reminds us how simple material realities of daily life become powerful images to describe spiritual realities: a belt that encircles the body illustrates how sin, servitude, or judgment can suffocate us. For the believer, it is also an invitation to reject anything that hinders us, to free ourselves from the yoke of slavery to walk in the freedom that Christ offers us.

sens: strip of fabric or leather that surrounds the waist to tighten clothing
symbol of strength and power in a man
H4206B.detail: 1. The belt is a strip of fabric or leather that one ties around the waist to hold and tighten clothing. In antiquity, it was a practical and common accessory. 2. Figuratively, the belt represents the strength and power of a man: 'loosing the belt of the mighty' (Job 12:21) means taking away a powerful man's authority and ability to act, as one would loosen his belt to weaken his hold and vigor.
H4206B.origine: This Hebrew word belongs to a small family of words designating the belt or war belt. The root verb evokes the idea of girding, tightening around. The belt was an element of clothing that was both practical and symbolic in the biblical world: it held the cloak and the loincloth in place, but it also signified the status and ability of a man to act and fight.
H4206B.emploi: This word appears only once in this sense in the Hebrew Bible. It is found in Job's discourse on the sovereignty of God: God 'loosens the belt of the mighty', meaning that He takes away the strength and authority of the powerful. The image is that of a warrior being disarmed by loosening his belt: he loses his balance, his poise, and his power to act.
H4206B.portee: This verse reminds the reader that all human strength, power, and authority are in God's hands. No strong man can rely solely on his own power: God can at any moment strip him of what supports him. It is a call to humility and recognition that our security comes from God, not from our own strength.

sens: Three-pronged utensil for retrieving meat from a cauldron
Instrument used to take one's share during the sacrifice
H4207A.detail:
1. The fork is a three-pronged kitchen utensil used to remove pieces of meat from a cooking vessel — cauldron, pot, or stew pot. In 1 Samuel 2:13-14, the servant of the priest uses it to scoop from the meat broth that is cooking and extract the portion intended for the priest.
2. This object takes on a symbolic dimension in the context of sacrificial worship: it is the instrument by which the servant of the priest dishonestly takes the meat from the sacrifice, even before the fat is offered to God. The fork thus becomes a symbol of the sacrilegious diversion committed by the priests of Shiloh.
H4207A.origine: The Hebrew word מַזְלֵג (mazleg) (with its variant מִזְלָגָה (mizlagah)) simply refers to a fork, as one would have in any ancient kitchen. The name comes from the image of its three prongs that pierce and hold. It is a utilitarian object, without theological background — but the Bible mentions it to illustrate the abuse of the priests.
H4207A.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Samuel 2:13-14. It describes the crucial moment when the priests of Shiloh, before the offering of the fat to God, take a personal share by poking into the cauldron with a three-pronged fork. The context shows that this practice had become systematic and scandalous: "This is how they acted toward all the Israelites who came there to Shiloh." The use of the term fork emphasizes the crude and predatory nature of the act.
H4207A.portee: This fork illustrates how the greed of the priests had corrupted worship. It reminds the reader that divine service requires integrity and that diverting, even a little, what is consecrated to God is a serious failing. It is a lesson on moral vigilance regarding offerings and generosity toward God.

sens: three-pronged instrument used to handle sacrifices on the altar
model or plan of this utensil
H4207B.detail:
1. The fork is a three-pronged cult utensil made of bronze, used by the priests to manipulate offerings and ashes on the altar of burnt offerings of the tabernacle and the temple. It is among the essential equipment for religious service: in Exodus 27:3, Moses commands to make "forks" of bronze for the altar, alongside ash pans, shovels, and basins.
2. The word also refers to the model or plan of this instrument, particularly when David hands over the plans for the temple to Solomon: in 1 Chronicles 28:17, the king receives the "model of the forks" in gold, which will serve as a reference for construction.
H4207B.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to pierce" or "to puncture," evoking the action of the utensil's sharp prongs. The fork is a practical handling tool: it allows the priest to manage the sacrifices without soiling his hands. A related form, מַזְלֵג (mazleg), is a variant or derivative of the same word.
H4207B.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Bible, always in connection with cultic equipment. It is found in descriptions of the tabernacle (Exodus 27:3 and 38:3), where it is listed among the utensils of the altar. It is mentioned in the instructions for transporting the tabernacle (Numbers 4:14), where the Levites must pack the fork with the other instruments. Finally, it appears in the transmission of the temple plans by David to Solomon (1 Chronicles 28:17) and in the realization of these plans (2 Chronicles 4:16). In each occurrence, it is the same practical utensil of sacrificial worship.
H4207B.portee: This word reminds us that Israelite worship was a material and concrete worship: God required specific tools, made with care and respect. These ordinary utensils, like the fork, held a particular holiness because they served the Lord's service. For today's believer, this illustrates that even the practical details of our service to God matter and require faithfulness.

sens: The constellations of stars grouped according to imaginary figures
The signs of the zodiac — twelve imaginary divisions of the sky through which the sun and planets pass
H4208.detail:
1. The word refers to the constellations, that is, the groups of stars that the ancients saw forming figures or designs in the night sky. The biblical example in 2 Kings 23:5 shows that this object of worship was associated with the worship of the stars.
2. More specifically, it likely refers to the twelve signs of the zodiac — the constellations that the sun traverses throughout the year and to which astrologers attributed influence over destinies. King Josiah abolished this worship as part of the superstitions imported from Babylon.
H4208.origine: The Hebrew word מַזָּלוֹת (mazzalot) may be related to Aramaic and ancient Babylonian. It comes from a root evoking fall or destiny: among the Mesopotamian peoples, astrologers believed that the stars and their arrangements "fell" or "stopped" on mortals to dictate their future. This term reflects the grip of Babylonian astrological thought on ancient Israel.
H4208.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 23:5, during the great religious reform of King Josiah in the 7th century BC. In this passage, the zodiac is mentioned among the objects of a form of heterodox worship — alongside the sun, the moon, and "all the host of heaven." This shows that astrology and the zodiac were part of the religious practices that idolatrous kings had introduced in Judah, likely under Babylonian influence. Josiah's reform aimed to purify the temple and Israel from these foreign superstitions.
H4208.portee: This word reminds us that the worship of the stars and reliance on astrology are presented in the Bible as deviations from the worship of the true God. While only the Lord masters the future, astrology claims that the constellations dominate our destinies. It is a call not to seek our security or direction in the signs of the heavens, but in the One who created the heavens and the stars.

sens: Project, plan formed by thought
Ability to reflect and understand
Intention, inner disposition of the heart
Evil project, plot
H4209.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a project or plan that someone forms in their mind: it is the fruit of reflection, what one proposes to do. In Proverbs 3:21, the son is urged to keep "the reflection," that is, the discernment that allows for wise planning.
2. By extension, it refers to the very ability to reflect, deliberate, and form judgments (Job 21:27: "your thoughts" that God reads in the heart).
3. The word applies to intention, the secret disposition of the heart, what one truly thinks (Psalms 10:4: "all his thoughts" of the wicked who denies God).
4. When the intention is evil, it becomes a criminal project, a plot: Psalms 139:20 speaks of those who "speak of you in a criminal manner," and Jeremiah 11:15 mentions "a multitude of crimes" committed in the house of God.
H4209.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to propose" or "to deliberate." It refers to the activity of the mind that thinks, that forms designs. Reflection implies a certain mastery and conscious intention: it is not an impulsive act, but something that is elaborated, that is matured.
H4209.emploi: This word appears 19 times, mostly in Psalms and Proverbs. In Proverbs, it is often an asset: "reflection" accompanies wisdom and discernment (Proverbs 1:4; 3:21; 8:12). But in Psalms, it often takes on a negative hue: these are the thoughts of the wicked, their plots against God and his servants (Psalms 10:4; 21:12; 139:20). Jeremiah uses it for the designs of God's own heart (Jeremiah 23:20; 30:24), but also for the crimes of Israel (Jeremiah 11:15).
H4209.portee: This word reminds us that our most secret thoughts — our reflections, our intentions, our plans — are not hidden from God. They can be a source of wisdom if we guide them by the fear of God, or a source of misfortune if we allow them to become corrupt. It is a call to guard our heart and our thoughts, for from there our actions arise.

sens: Musical composition intended to be sung, generally a religious hymn
Poem or prayer adorned with a lyrical and musical form
H4210.detail:
1. A hymn is primarily a melody, a musical composition that is sung. In the Bible, hymns are the poems found in the collection of Psalms, each designed to be sung as a prayer or praise to God. The word appears in the titles of the Psalms ("A Psalm of David", Psalms 23:1) to indicate to the reader the literary genre and the purpose of the text.

2. Beyond the simple melody, a hymn is a prayer adorned with poetic beauty. It is a genre that combines meaningful words with a musical form, allowing the singer to express their heart, faith, trust, or repentance. The hymns of the Psalms address serious subjects: God's protection (Psalms 23:1), confession of sin (Psalms 51:1), the call for divine help (Psalms 4:1).
H4210.origine: The Hebrew word mizmor (מִזְמוֹר) comes from a root meaning "to play a stringed instrument." It originally evokes the idea of making a harp or lyre resonate. The word first designates the musical sound, then the sung poem itself. It is a term specifically related to the worship of the temple in Jerusalem and to Israelite religious practice.
H4210.emploi: The word "hymn" appears 57 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively as a title or introduction to the Psalms. It is a characteristic word of psalmic language: it is found at the beginning of 53 different psalms, from Psalm 3 to Psalm 143. It designates the literary genre of the collection of Psalms, a collection of sung prayers. Some psalms bear other titles or complementary names, but "hymn" is the most common. Its usage in the Bible is therefore very specialized: it exclusively refers to this type of religious composition intended for worship.
H4210.portee: For the believer, the word "hymn" reminds us that prayer is not merely a private or silent matter, but also a common, joyful, and musical expression of faith. The Psalms show us that singing is an appropriate and even preferred way to address God: it connects the heart, body, and community. By singing the biblical hymns, the Christian joins millennia of prayer and appropriates the inspired words of Scripture.

sens: Curved cutting tool used for pruning and harvesting the fruits of the vine
Weapon of war converted into an agricultural instrument
Weapon forged from a tool of peace
H4211.detail:
1. The sickle is an agricultural tool with a curved, sharp blade, used to cut the vine shoots and harvest grapes: in Isaiah 18:5, it is seen in action, cutting the shoots and slicing the stems when the grapes begin to ripen. It is the instrument of the vine grower.
2. In the vision of peace in Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3, sickles symbolize tools of life: nations transform their war spears into sickles to cultivate the land. It is the biblical image of disarmament and peace: instead of killing, one harvests.
3. Conversely, in Joel 3:10, it is the opposite: the plowshares and sickles are reforged into weapons of war, swords, and spears. The text shows how instruments of peace become instruments of violence, reflecting the human heart that shifts from work to war.
H4211.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to cut" or "to trim." It is a concrete noun that designates the tool itself by its function: it is used for pruning, trimming, and harvesting. In the Greek Old Testament, this word corresponds to a term designating the instrument of the vine grower, showing that sickle and vineyard go together.
H4211.emploi: The word appears only four times in biblical Hebrew, always related to vineyard work or the transformation of weapons. Three occurrences (Isaiah 2:4, Micah 4:3, Joel 3:10) group the same verse or nearly so: it is a prophetic peace text that circulates and returns, showing its theological weight. One occurrence (Isaiah 18:5) shows it in action during the grape harvest. The sickle is therefore the tool of the vintage and the symbol of the conversion of weapons into tools of life.
H4211.portee: The sickle teaches that peace is not simply the absence of war: it is the conversion of the human heart, transforming what was used to destroy into what serves to nourish. For the Christian, this passage invites reflection on whether their hands, thoughts, and energies are directed towards death or life, towards harvest or violence.

sens: Small metal utensil used to trim the wicks of the temple lamps
Tool used in worship for the maintenance of the sanctuary
H4212.detail: 1. The temple knife is a small instrument made of gold or bronze, intended to cut or shorten the wicks of the lamps that burned continuously in the sanctuary. It is an ordinary service tool, but consecrated to worship: in 1 Kings 7:50 and 2 Chronicles 4:22, it is listed among the gold furnishings of Solomon's temple, alongside basins and bowls. 2. More broadly, it is a utensil of public worship in the temple of Jerusalem. All passages (1 Kings 7:50; 2 Kings 12:13; 2 Kings 25:14; 2 Chronicles 4:22; Jeremiah 52:18) mention it in lists of temple objects, sometimes in bronze when referring to ordinary maintenance equipment.
H4212.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to cut" or "to slice." It literally designates the instrument that cuts. This type of tool was essential for the worship of the sanctuary to keep the lamps in good working order.
H4212.emploi: The word "knife" (temple knife) appears 5 times in the Bible, always to designate utensils of worship. In 1 Kings 7:50 and 2 Chronicles 4:22, it is included in the description of Solomon's temple, made of pure gold. In 2 Kings 12:13, it specifies that none were made of silver for the repaired temple. In 2 Kings 25:14 and Jeremiah 52:18, at the time of the temple's destruction by Babylon, the bronze utensils taken are enumerated, including these knives. The tool thus appears in contexts of the establishment and management of the sanctuary.
H4212.portee: This modest utensil reminds us that the worship of the God of Israel requires order, regularity, and attention to detail. Nothing was left to chance in the service of the temple: each object had its function and its place. For the believer, it is a reminder that serving God also means cultivating faithfulness in the small things.

sens: A short duration, a limited period of time
A minimal quantity, very little of something
A reduced number of people or objects that remain
H4213.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a short duration, a brief delay: "Yet a little while, and the punishment will cease" (Isaiah 10:25). It conveys the idea of a moment that passes quickly, a period that can be counted on fingers.
2. It can also signify a very minimal quantity or portion, almost negligible: "What remains will be little, almost nothing" (Isaiah 16:14). The image is that of what is left when everything has been taken, an insignificant residue.
3. Finally, it applies to a limited number of people or things — a remnant, a small group: "And there remains only a small number" (Isaiah 24:6). It is what survives after destruction or reduction.
H4213.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to be small" or "to be few." It expresses the idea of smallness, limitation, whether regarding duration, quantity, or number. It is a concrete term that describes what is reduced, restricted, limited in its dimensions or extent.
H4213.emploi: The word appears four times in Isaiah, always in contexts of judgment or divine promise. It is used to measure the time remaining before a decisive event: the punishment that will soon cease (Isaiah 10:25), the transformation of Lebanon into a garden (Isaiah 29:17). It also measures the consequences of judgment: what remains of the people of Moab (Isaiah 16:14) or of the devastated land (Isaiah 24:6). It is always a word of limitation that creates tension between present destruction and the expectation of what is to come.
H4213.portee: This word reminds the believer that difficulties, judgments, and periods of trial last "only a little while" — there is a limit to suffering and evil. At the same time, it emphasizes the rarity of the faithful remnant: those who remain after judgment form a small group. It is both a message of hope (it will not last) and humility (we are but a handful).

sens: A fork or flat shovel used to separate grain from chaff by tossing it into the air
The action of winnowing, that is, sifting grain to purify it
Biblical image of divine judgment that separates the good from the bad
H4214.detail: 1. The winnowing fork is an agricultural tool, a fork or flat shovel used to winnow grain: the grain is tossed into the air, the wind carries away the light chaff, and the pure grain falls back down. In Isaiah 30:24, this "winnowing fork" is a piece of harvest equipment, the concrete instrument of farmers. 2. The verb "to winnow" describes the action itself of sifting grain. It is a repetitive, necessary task: without winnowing, one cannot separate the grain from the chaff. 3. The Bible uses this image to speak of God's judgment: in Jeremiah 15:7, the Lord says, "I winnow them with the wind," meaning He separates, judges His people by scattering the rebels. Just as the wind blows away the chaff, divine justice separates those who obey from those who turn away.
H4214.origine: The Hebrew word מִזְרֶה (miz.reh) comes from the root זָרָה (zarah), which means "to scatter" or "to disperse." This root evokes the action of the wind that scatters light things. The winnowing fork is thus named after this primary gesture: to scatter the chaff so that it flies away.
H4214.emploi: The word miz.reh appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in an agricultural or judgment context. In Isaiah 30:24, it is an instrument of the daily work of farmers. In Jeremiah 15:7, God speaks of winnowing His people, transforming the concrete tool into a prophetic image of judgment: God separates and scatters as one separates grain from chaff. These two uses show how the Bible moves from agricultural realism to the theology of divine judgment.
H4214.portee: The winnowing fork reminds the reader that God's judgment is real and effective: it separates the good from the bad just as one separates grain from chaff. It is an image that invites awareness that our life here is under God's gaze, who distinguishes those who follow Him from those who turn away. This image, far from being abstract, speaks a language that every ancient reader understood: that of necessary work and sorting.

sens: a violent air current that scatters and disperses
H4215.detail: 1. The word denotes a powerful wind that scatters, that disperses — in this case, in the context of Job 37:9, the cold north wind that brings storms and sweeps everything in its path. It is the very image of the brute force of nature, capable of fragmenting and dispersing whatever it encounters.
H4215.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root זָרָה (zarah), which means "to disperse," "to scatter"; it is found in words that express the action of sifting grain, of sifting, of throwing to the wind. The form מְזָרֶה (me-zarah) is constructed with the prefix indicating the instrument or agent: literally, "that which disperses." It is a word that retains the very concrete image of the action of spreading, of putting into disorder.
H4215.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 37:9, where Elihu describes the meteorological phenomena that manifest God's power. He speaks of the north wind that brings cold and storm — a scattering, chaotic, destructive wind. It is in a context of divine revelation: the brute forces of nature reveal the majesty and power of the One who commands them.
H4215.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that even the chaotic and destructive forces of nature — the wind that scatters, the storm that devastates — are under God's sovereign control. It invites us to recognize behind natural phenomena the wisdom and divine power, and to seek in the disorders of creation the signs of His mastery.

sens: The twelve constellations that mark the sun's path in the sky
The complete set of astrological signs and the stars that compose them
H4216.detail:
1. The zodiac refers to the twelve visible constellations in the night sky that the sun seems to traverse throughout the year. It is a band of sky divided into regular zones, each named after a characteristic constellation. In Job 38:32, God asks Job if he can make "the signs of the zodiac appear in their season," meaning govern the regular and precise appearance of these constellations throughout the seasons.
2. The word also refers to the complete set of thirty-six constellations associated with the twelve main zodiac signs. These celestial divisions have been used since antiquity to measure time and guide travelers, although the Bible never recommends them as a basis for predicting the future.
H4216.origine: The Hebrew word mazzarah comes from a root meaning "to shine" or "to radiate." It denotes what shines in the firmament — the visible constellations. Although this term is rare in the Bible (only one occurrence), it shows that the ancient Hebrews were aware of the existence of these celestial divisions. The context of the book of Job, with its references to stars and celestial bodies, reflects the interest that ancient cosmology had in the organization of the night sky.
H4216.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 38:32. It is found in God's long discourse to Job, where the Lord enumerates the wonders of creation and questions Job about his ability to govern them. God successively mentions the Pleiades, Orion, the Big Dipper, and the zodiac, each constellation illustrating the power and order that God has established in the universe. This unique mention shows that the zodiac was a known celestial landmark to the ancients, without the Bible approving or disapproving of it. It simply uses it as an example of the marvelous order of the cosmos.
H4216.portee: This mention of the zodiac reminds the believer that God controls every aspect of creation, even the most distant constellations. The passage invites admiration for the order and precision of the cosmos as a testimony to divine wisdom, rather than seeking in it omens or predictions. It also highlights the humility we should feel in the face of the mysteries of the universe that only God fully controls.

sens: Direction of the rising sun, where the sun rises
The gate or region that faces the east
H4217G.detail:
1. The east refers to the direction where the sun rises, that is, the east. It is the fundamental cardinal point for the ancient Hebrews: in Hebrew, the word comes directly from the image of the sun that rises, that emerges. When one turns towards the temple in Jerusalem, the east is naturally in front of them.
2. The east gate is one of the gates of Jerusalem, the one that opens towards the east. In Nehemiah 3:29, Schemaiah was responsible for guarding and maintaining it during the reconstruction of the city's walls after the exile.
H4217G.origine: The Hebrew word mizrach comes from the root zarach (זרח), which means "to rise, shine, go out." It is the image of the sun rising on the horizon each morning. The word thus primarily designates what concerns the rising of the sun, and by extension, the direction of the east. The Hebrews viewed geography from the east: this is why the east was the main reference point, as we often see in the Old Testament.
H4217G.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible in Nehemiah 3:29, in the context of the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile (circa 445 B.C.). It designates here the east gate, one of the main entrances to the city. This gate was strategically important, as it provided access beyond the Jordan and to the lands of the east. The context shows that it was an essential element of the fortifications of Jerusalem that needed to be restored and monitored.
H4217G.portee: For the Christian, this gate reminds us of the importance of sacred geography in the Old Testament. The east, the direction of the rising sun, traditionally symbolizes expectation, hope, and the coming of God. Meditating on the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem, of which the east gate was a key element, also speaks of the renewal of God's people after trial.

sens: The place where the sun rises, the cardinal point east
The direction towards this cardinal point
A region or territory located to the east
One of the four cardinal directions used to describe boundaries and borders
H4217H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the place of the rising sun, the spot where it rises each morning — this is the most concrete meaning. Thus, the eastern limit of the courtyard of the Tabernacle was called "the side of the east" (Exodus 27:13), simply marking the direction of the rising sun.
2. By extension, it is the direction itself, the orientation towards the east. When the Bible says that the sons of Joseph extended "toward the waters of Jericho, to the east" (Joshua 16:1), it indicates the direction in which their territory extended.
3. The word can also designate an entire region located to the east of a reference point. Thus, Moses saw "all the plain across the Jordan, to the east" (Deuteronomy 4:49), meaning the eastern region beyond the river.
4. In lists of territorial boundaries, the east appears as one of the four cardinal points to precisely delineate a terrain. The Psalms speak of gathering the peoples "from the east and from the west, from the north and from the sea" (Psalms 107:3), where east and west designate the eastern and western extremities of the known world.
H4217H.origine: The Hebrew word mizrach comes from the root zarah, which means "to rise, shine" — the image of the sun rising. This is why mizrach literally designates the "rising" of the sun, and thus the east, the direction of the rising. All biblical usages revolve around this idea of a direction or a place defined by the movement of the rising sun.
H4217H.emploi: This word appears 70 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in historical and geographical books: Joshua (for the boundaries of tribal territories), Kings and Chronicles (for the architecture of the Temple), and Psalms and Prophets (for cosmic or theological imagery). It frequently accompanies the word "side" (tsad): "from the side of the east" to designate a face or a boundary. In Exodus and Numbers, it situates the encampments and altars. In Isaiah and the other prophets, "the east" can designate a people or a power coming from the east (Isaiah 41:2, 41:25), or serve in eschatological visions. The meaning remains always geographical or directive, never abstract.
H4217H.portee: This word reminds us that biblical geography is not abstract: it is lived, measurable, linked to visible cardinal points. For the reader, recognizing these orientations helps to better understand the territories spoken of in the Bible and to grasp how space was organized. Moreover, the east holds a particular significance in Scripture: it is from where salvation and light come, the east symbolizes the renewal and hope of God who comes to enlighten His people.

sens: Land intended for sowing
Act or time of sowing
Set of seeds sown
H4218.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the land where one sows: it is the plot of land prepared to receive the seeds. In Isaiah 19:7, it refers to the lands along the Nile, usually fertile and suitable for cultivation — these sowing fields that dry up when the river recedes.
2. By extension, the word can also describe the act of sowing or the season of sowing: the moment when the farmer entrusts his seeds to the earth.
3. Finally, it can designate the seeds themselves that are sown, as a set intended to grow.
H4218.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root זרע (zara), which means "to sow." This root evokes the fundamental action of the farmer: to spread the seeds. It also gives the word זֶרַע (zera), which means "seed" or "offspring" — the seed in both a literal and figurative sense. The prefix מ (mi) transforms the verb into a concrete noun: the place or act of sowing.
H4218.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 19:7. The prophet describes one of the plagues of Egypt: the Nile does not rise, and the sowing lands, normally watered by the floods, dry up. The context emphasizes the dependence of the Egyptian farmer on the river: his sowing fields are doomed to sterility and ruin if the water fails.
H4218.portee: This passage reminds us that all fertility comes from God, not from our own strength. The sower entrusts his seeds to the earth, but only the Lord gives the rain and the harvest. It is an invitation to trust and to give thanks to the Giver of all life.

sens: Metal container, generally made of silver or gold, intended to hold or pour liquids in worship.
Cup or vessel used for drinking or making libations (liquid offerings to God).
Container used to collect the blood of sacrifices or the ashes from the altar.
H4219.detail:
1. The basin is primarily a worship utensil, made of precious metals (silver, gold, bronze). It serves to hold and transfer liquids — water, wine, or oil — during sacrifices and religious ceremonies. Thus, in the description of the tabernacle, Exodus 27:3 lists basins among the utensils necessary for the altar, where they help collect ashes or pour libations. The twelve princes of Israel offer them at the dedication of the altar (Numbers 7:25, 7:84), affirming their commitment to worship.
2. The basin can also refer to a drinking cup, particularly for wine or libations. It is in this sense that 2 Chronicles 4:22 lists the gold "cups" of the temple alongside other sacred vessels, and that 2 Kings 12:13 mentions the silver or gold "cups" that were not made from certain temple funds.
3. By extension, the basin also symbolizes the blood shed in sacrificial worship — the blood that is collected or poured into it — making visible and concrete the offering made to God. This is why Amos 6:6 and Zechariah 14:20 mention basins in images of judgment or final sanctification.
H4219.origine: The Hebrew word מִזְרָק (mizraq) derives from a root meaning "to throw" or "to pour": the basin is etymologically the "vessel for pouring." This image of pouring is central to its meaning — they are not merely inert containers, but instruments of action, through which water, wine, or blood is poured in honor of God. The word belongs to the specific vocabulary of temple worship, just like dishes (qe'arah), cups (kos), and sacred spoons.
H4219.emploi: The word mizraq appears thirty-two times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively to describe the worship of the tabernacle and the temple. It appears prominently in Numbers 7, where the twelve princes of Israel offer silver basins at the dedication of the altar — a solemn repetition that underscores the importance of the basin among the offerings. It reappears in the descriptions of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 7, 2 Chronicles 4) and in the inventories of worship utensils (Exodus 27, 38; 1 Chronicles 28). Jeremiah 52:18-19 lists the basins taken during the destruction of the temple in 586 B.C., attesting that these objects truly existed and retained their symbolic value. Once, in Amos 6:6 and Zechariah 9:15, 14:20, the basin enters into figurative language of judgment or eschatological blessing.
H4219.portee: The basin reminds us that worship is not abstract: it is carried out through material objects, carefully crafted from precious metals, which embody the seriousness and reverence of the people towards God. Each basin offered at the dedication of the tabernacle expresses the personal commitment of a prince of Israel, showing that faith is made concrete in giving. These utensils also remind us that sacrifices — the heart of Old Testament worship — involve the pouring of blood, a solemn and mysterious action, mediated by humble objects that made it visible to the entire community.

sens: Well-fed, plump, and fat animal suitable for sacrifice
Valuable property, rich possession (by figurative extension)
H4220.detail: 1. The word designates a fat and well-fed animal, particularly capable of serving as a sacrifice. In Psalms 66:15, the psalmist promises the Lord "fat sheep as burnt offerings, with the fat of rams": these are generous beasts in meat and fat, thus precious, offered as a sign of gratitude and obedience. 2. By extension, the word can evoke a rich and abundant possession, concrete wealth. In Isaiah 5:17, it speaks of the "ruined possessions of the rich": here, the term suggests envied and abundant material goods that will be abandoned to strangers.
H4220.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that naturally designates what is fat, plump, well-fleshed. The fat animal was a sign of prosperity and health in a pastoral context: a "fat" beast showed that its owner possessed resources and good land. Hence its use to evoke wealth and abundance more broadly.
H4220.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. In Psalms 66:15, it qualifies the sheep offered in sacrifice, emphasizing their quality and value. In Isaiah 5:17, it indirectly describes the possessions of the "rich" to which the sheep will graze, used ironically to show how the wealth of the Northern Kingdom of Israel, a symbol of human pride, will be abandoned to a humble fate.
H4220.portee: This word reminds us that the authentic sacrifice offered to God must be generous and costly: we do not give to the Lord what costs us nothing. It also invites the reader to reflect on material goods: human wealth, however envied, is fragile and perishable in the face of God's judgment.

sens: White and fatty substance contained within the bones
H4221.detail: 1. The marrow is the soft and fatty material that fills the interior of the bones. It circulates there and nourishes the bone itself. In Job 21:24, the healthy man has "his bones filled with marrow": this physical detail illustrates his abundance of life and strength, showing someone well-nourished and vigorous.
H4221.origine: The Hebrew word מֹחַ (mo'ach) specifically designates bone marrow. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of what is tender and soft inside. In Hebrew, this word has few variations in its family, as it designates a precise and well-identified biological reality.
H4221.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 21:24. Job describes a prosperous man in excellent physical health: his bones are filled with marrow, his marrow abounds. This detail underscores the vital fullness of the wicked to whom Job alludes, reinforcing his argument about the apparent prosperity of the wicked.
H4221.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible speaks of the human body with realism and respect. The marrow, hidden at the heart of the bone, symbolizes inner vitality: it invites us not to judge someone solely on their external appearances, but to recognize that true life and true strength come from within, from what God fills in us.

sens: striking one's hands together
applauding, expressing joy through this gesture
manifesting exultation, disdain, or triumph
H4222.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: striking one's hands together. It is a physical gesture of the body, like when one applauds. In Isaiah 55:12, the mountains and hills "will clap their hands" for joy at Israel's departure, a poetic image where creation itself expresses its joy.

2. In a positive context, clapping hands means to applaud, to express joy and enthusiasm. In Psalms 98:8, the psalmist calls the rivers to clap their hands to celebrate the Lord: it is a cry of joy, a way of saying that all of nature rejoices.

3. The same gesture can also express malicious exultation, wicked triumph, or disdain. In Ezekiel 25:6, the neighboring people clap their hands and stomp their feet in delight at Israel's misfortune: the gesture reveals the wickedness of the heart, the evil satisfaction in the suffering of others.
H4222.origine: The Hebrew verb מָחָא comes from a root expressing the action of striking or hitting. In Aramaic, the parallel form מְחָא means "to strike" in a more general sense. The word describes the sound and movement of the gesture: the hands striking against each other produce a sharp and loud sound, hence the meaning to applaud or to express an emotion loudly.
H4222.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Old Testament. In Psalms and Isaiah, it is used in the context of joyful celebration: creation itself is invited to clap its hands to praise God (see Psalms 98:8 and Isaiah 55:12). In Ezekiel 25:6, the same verb describes the mocking triumphant gesture of the Ammonites who rejoice at Israel's fate. The verb thus changes tone according to the hearts: it can be a hymn of praise or the expression of cruel joy, showing that the gesture itself is neutral; it is the intention that colors it.
H4222.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize that authentic joy is expressed visibly and freely, including through the body. Clapping hands before God is to manifest outwardly what the heart feels. But the word also warns: the same gesture can reveal the absence of love for one's neighbor if one rejoices in their misfortune. True Christian joy is never built on the suffering of others.

sens: to hit violently someone or something
to reach something decisively
to oppose, resist someone
H4223.detail:
1. To hit violently someone or something: the word primarily denotes the physical action of striking, inflicting a blow. In Daniel 2:34, a stone "struck the feet of iron and clay of the statue," meaning it hit them violently to break them.
2. To reach something decisively: the blow struck achieves its goal and produces a visible and lasting effect. In Daniel 2:35, the stone that "had struck the statue" completely destroyed it, so that it became a great mountain that "filled the whole earth."
3. To oppose, resist someone: figuratively, it means to stand up to, to obstruct someone. In Daniel 4:35, "there is no one who can resist His hand" — no one can oppose God's hand or contradict Him.
H4223.origine: The Aramaic verb מְחָא comes from a root that expresses the idea of striking, giving a blow. The basic meaning is the violent action that reaches its target. Depending on the grammatical form used, the verb can also mean "to obstruct" or "to prevent": it is the same root, but applied to stopping or thwarting someone rather than physically striking them.
H4223.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears 4 times in the Bible, only in the Aramaic portions of Daniel and Ezra (chapters 2 to 7 of Daniel and chapter 6 of Ezra). In Daniel 2:34-35, it describes the stone that strikes and destroys the statue — a symbolic event of the destruction of earthly kingdoms by the Kingdom of God. In Ezra 6:11, it takes on the figurative meaning of "to attach" to wood (to hang), meaning to inflict physical punishment. In Daniel 4:35, it means "to resist" or "to oppose" the power of God. The context shows that the word is used to express either a concrete violent action or, figuratively, an opposition or hindrance.
H4223.portee: This word reminds us of God's sovereign power: the one who strikes with authority is the one who masters events. In Daniel's vision, the stone that strikes the earthly kingdoms symbolizes the irresistible establishment of the Kingdom of God. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize that no one can resist God and that His will is accomplished infallibly, even when it destroys what seemed powerful.

sens: protection against the elements or danger
refuge, a safe place to take cover
H4224A.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a concrete protection against wind, rain, or storms — a place that protects the physical body. In Isaiah 32:2, a righteous king is compared to a "shelter against the wind" and a "refuge against the storm," images that show how a true leader protects his people from external threats, just as a rock or a stream saves the traveler in the desert.
2. Figuratively, the shelter becomes a spiritual or moral protection — a place of inner security, a refuge where one can rest and escape danger. It is the idea that someone righteous, or trust in God, offers us this invisible yet real protection.
H4224A.origine: The word comes from the root חבא (khaba), which means "to hide" or "to conceal." A shelter is thus literally a place where one hides, where one takes cover. This same family of words appears in the Old Testament to express the idea of refuge or hiding place — a secret and protected place.
H4224A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 32:2, where the prophet describes a king who reigns with justice. In this passage, Isaiah uses the image of the shelter to show how a good ruler protects his people. The context is that of a messianic promise: when a true leader reigns, he will be for his people what a shelter is for a lost traveler — an absolute and reliable protection.
H4224A.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that true security comes from external protection — whether human (a just leader) or divine (God Himself). In a life traversed by storms and dangers, seeking shelter is not a weakness, but wisdom. Jesus, the promise and fulfillment of this righteous king, becomes the ultimate shelter for all who trust in Him.

sens: a place where one hides
refuge
asylum
H4224B.detail:
1. The word denotes a physical, hidden place where someone takes refuge to escape danger. In 1 Samuel 23:23, David asks his men to explore all the places where Saul might be hiding: it is a den, a secret lodging in the mountains or caves.
2. By extension, it is a safe refuge, a place of protection — not just a hole to hide in, but a place to find asylum and security against a threat or pursuer.
H4224B.origine: The word comes from the root חבא (khaba), which means "to hide" or "to conceal." The prefix מ (ma) makes it a noun of action or place: literally "that which is hidden" or "the action of hiding." The same root also gives מַחְבֵא (maḥbé), which has the same meaning. The basic image is that of secrecy, the act of covering or veiling oneself.
H4224B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Samuel 23:23. In this context, David is pursued by Saul and must take refuge in the natural shelters of the kingdom. The term "places" (of hiding) describes the shelters that Saul seeks to explore to track David down. It is a very concrete word, related to survival and fleeing from an imminent threat.
H4224B.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible acknowledges trials, fleeing, moments when the believer must take refuge. David, the man after God's own heart, had to flee and hide — it is a humble reality of the life of faith. The text also emphasizes that even when one hides, even in secret shelters, God sees and knows. It is an invitation to seek in God, not only a material hiding place but authentic protection.

sens: That which unites two elements by joining them together
Specific point where two things meet and assemble
Edge of a piece of fabric intended to be attached to another
H4225.detail:
1. The word concretely refers to the action and result of joining two elements. In the construction of the Tabernacle, "jointure" or "assembly" describes the place where two pieces of fabric (the curtains) touch and unite through blue cords (Exodus 26:4). It is the technical area of connection.
2. More broadly, it is the physical meeting point where two parts become a single structure. When it comes to the ephod (the garment of the high priest), the gold rings are placed "at the jointure" (Exodus 28:27), meaning exactly where the two shoulder pieces meet.
3. By extension, the word can refer to the very edge of a piece that must be joined to another — the end that "finishes" the assembly, the one that receives the fastening cords.
H4225.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to join" or "to assemble." It describes the concrete action of bringing together several distinct elements to form a coherent whole, a central idea in the construction of the Tabernacle where every detail had to fit perfectly according to the divine plan.
H4225.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Bible, exclusively in the context of the construction of the Tabernacle (especially Exodus 26 and 36, with one occurrence in Exodus 28 and 39). In Exodus 26:4-5 and 36:11-12, it refers to the points where the curtains of the Tabernacle are joined by means of cords: these are functional and decorative "jointures." In Exodus 28:27, the word applies to the anatomical junction of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, where the gold rings are attached. The context is always technical and liturgical: it is the precise and orderly union of distinct pieces into a harmonious whole.
H4225.portee: This word reminds the believer that the Tabernacle was built according to an extremely precise order, where each jointure had its importance. This attention to the details of assembly symbolizes the harmony and unity that should be sought in the people of God, where each has its place and contributes to the whole. The jointure also reminds us that true union only arises when distinct parts agree to be linked together according to a greater design.

sens: Metal piece that assembles or connects two parts
Structural element that consolidates a construction
H4226.detail:
1. A crampon is a metal piece — usually iron or bronze — that serves to connect and hold together two elements, such as the leaves of a door (1 Chronicles 22:3). It is a connector, a link that prevents the pieces from separating.
2. More broadly, the word refers to any structural element that consolidates a construction: beam, tie, or bracing that holds a building together (2 Chronicles 34:11). The image is that of a firm grip that keeps the whole intact.
H4226.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to bind" or "to attach together." The same root appears in words denoting ties, knots, or assemblies. The word fundamentally evokes the action of joining, putting together to form a solid unit.
H4226.emploi: This word appears twice in the Bible, both in Chronicles and both in the context of the restoration of the Temple. In 1 Chronicles 22:3, David gathers iron to make crampons for the doors of the future Temple. In 2 Chronicles 34:11, King Josiah purchases beams and assembly wood for the restoration of the Temple. Both occurrences describe materials and construction techniques, reflecting the care taken to build a durable house.
H4226.portee: This small detail shows that the construction of the Temple is never neglected: every piece, even minor, is planned, costly, and important. It reminds us that the solidity of a divine work comes from attention to detail and the quality of assembly.

sens: Flat cooking utensil, made of metal, used for cooking food
Flat surface on which bread and cakes are prepared or baked
Metal plate used as a symbol in a prophetic vision
H4227.detail:
1. The poêle is a cooking utensil with low edges, used to cook food with direct heat. In offerings to God, it allows for the preparation of cakes made from flour kneaded with oil, baked without leaven (Leviticus 2:5). It is an essential piece of equipment for worship, used by the priests to transform ingredients into consecrated food.
2. The poêle can also refer to the cake or bread itself, the finished product rather than the utensil (1 Chronicles 23:29). The word is then used for the bread offered in worship, especially the cakes baked on the plate.
3. In Ezekiel's vision, an iron poêle becomes a prophetic symbol: placed between the prophet and Jerusalem, it represents the impending siege of the city (Ezekiel 4:3). Here, the ordinary object becomes an instrument of divine teaching.
H4227.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to dig" or "to deepen," hence the idea of a hollow container. The poêle is literally a hollow or curved surface, lightweight and manageable, different from an oven or grill. It is a well-known domestic and cultic utensil from the ancient world.
H4227.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Bible, mostly in the laws of offerings (Leviticus 2, 6, 7). It describes the tool with which the grain offerings to God are prepared, an important step in Levitical worship. Once only, in Ezekiel 4:3, it steps out of its culinary context to become an accessory of a symbolic act of prophecy: the iron poêle serves to represent the siege of Jerusalem. The word thus moves from the profane and liturgical domain to the prophetic domain.
H4227.portee: The poêle reminds us that divine worship engaged all the details of life: food, utensils, daily actions were consecrated and offered to God. The Christian understands that even ordinary acts of life can be sacred when done with sincerity and for the glory of God. The use of the poêle in prophecy also shows how God uses familiar objects to speak to His people.

sens: strip of fabric or leather that wraps around the waist
that which encircles, envelops, or constricts
symbol of strength, dignity, or social status
H4228.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a physical belt: a strip of fabric or leather tied around the waist to hold up clothing or for ornamentation. In Isaiah 3:24, the prophecy of judgment contrasts the adornments of proud women with the destitution of humiliation: instead of an elegant belt (or a 'wide' mantle in the translation), women will wear a simple rope. Thus, the belt was an element of attire that marked appearance and social rank.
2. Figuratively, that which encircles or envelops: the word describes the action of surrounding or tightening, as one would do with a rope or band. It is the image of a bond that holds or restrains.
3. Symbolically, the belt evokes strength, dignity, and status: it is an element of distinguished attire, and its absence or replacement by a coarse rope signifies degradation and shame.
H4228.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root חגר (hagur), which means 'to gird' or 'to surround'. It is found in words that describe the action of girding the loins, surrounding oneself, or preparing for action (notably in contexts of strength or preparation for battle). The masculine form of the same word also denotes a belt. The basic image is thus that of a band wrapped around the body, which holds and adorns.
H4228.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 3:24. This passage is an oracle of judgment in which the prophet Isaiah enumerates the punishments that the women of Jerusalem will suffer: their ornaments will be replaced by signs of mourning and humiliation. The 'wide' or elegant belt of prosperous times will be replaced by a coarse 'rope'. This context of reversal of fortunes shows that the belt embodies the luxury and dignity of a prosperous life, which judgment will destroy. The singular usage emphasizes the symbolic importance of clothing in the biblical imagination of shame and glory.
H4228.portee: This word reminds us that in biblical thought, clothing and adornments are not merely material objects: they express dignity, status, and self-esteem. Isaiah's prophecy invites the reader not to trust in appearance or external wealth, which will vanish on the day of judgment. It calls for a conversion of the heart rather than pride in adornment, reminding us that only the fear of God grants true dignity.

sens: Remove a trace, a mark, by rubbing or cleaning
Delete, annul as if erasing
Make disappear, completely exterminate
Voluntarily forget, set aside
Remove from memory or records, let fall into oblivion
H4229A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to erase a trace, a writing, as one wipes a surface. In Isaiah 25:8, God 'wipes away the tears from all faces' — He removes them from the face to console.
2. To erase also means to eliminate, annihilate: not only to remove a visible mark but to make it completely disappear, as if nothing existed. In Genesis 6:7, the Lord says: 'I will wipe out from the face of the earth the man I have created' — humans will be erased from creation.
3. By extension, to erase a person or their descendants means to eliminate them: in Psalms 109:13, the descendants of the wicked are 'exterminated'.
4. To erase can mean to forget: what is erased from memory, from consciousness, no longer counts. In Nehemiah 13:14, Nehemiah prays to God not to forget his deeds.
5. To erase from records or from heaven means to remove someone from the realm of the living or the elect: in Exodus 32:33, God says 'I will erase from my book' the one who has sinned; in Deuteronomy 29:20, the Lord 'will erase his name from under heaven'.
H4229A.origine: The Hebrew verb מָחָה (makhah) comes from a root that primarily evokes the physical action: to rub, clean, remove. Its primary image is that of rubbing away a trace. The word family includes terms related to erasure and disappearance. This verb is used for both a material gesture (wiping away tears) and for spiritual or moral realities (erasing a sin, a name).
H4229A.emploi: The verb מָחָה appears about 30 times in the Old Testament. It is first used in contexts of judgment: God 'exterminates' humans during the flood (Genesis 6:7), 'erases' sinners from the book (Exodus 32:33), removes a cursed lineage (Deuteronomy 25:6). It also denotes the action of forgetting or not retaining (Nehemiah 13:14). Sometimes it is physical and concrete: wiping away tears (Isaiah 25:8) or making a stain disappear. In Psalms 51, the psalmist asks God to 'erase' his transgressions — an image of forgiveness and moral purification. The word can also signify the definitive destruction of a memory (Psalms 109:13).
H4229A.portee: This word opens a depth on God's justice and forgiveness: it shows that God can 'erase' sin, remove it from the records, as if it had never existed. But to erase can also mean 'to exterminate' — the same gesture that consoles wipes away tears (Isaiah 25:8) can annihilate (Genesis 6:7). For the believer, the word invites us to understand that in Jesus, God 'erases' our sins (according to Isaiah 43:25), not by forgetting, but by an act of grace that restores us. It is a powerful image of forgiveness: not simply to forgive, but to make disappear, as if sin had never sullied our destiny.

sens: Progress along a line, a direction, a boundary
Unfold parallel to something
H4229B.detail:
1. The verb describes the movement of a line that advances following the outline of another: the boundary of the territory of Israel 'descends' from Schepham to Riblah, then 'extends along' the Sea of Kinnereth (Numbers 34:11). It is like tracing a boundary along a coast or bank.
2. In a broader sense, the word evokes the idea of progressing, advancing while keeping in contact with a given direction. In this technical passage describing boundaries, one must draw lines that follow the contours of the terrain.
H4229B.origine: The root חכ (mâchâh) means properly 'to strike' or 'to hit', which evokes the action of marking, tracing a boundary by marking it. The usage in Numbers 34:11 reflects the derived sense of 'to extend' or 'to progress in line', as if one were tracing a boundary line by marking it on the ground. This noun is rare in the Bible: it is mostly found in passages delineating the promised lands.
H4229B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew text of the Segond, in Numbers 34:11, in the precise context of describing the boundaries of the territory of Israel at the exit from Egypt. Moses enumerates the limits of the promised land according to the twelve tribes, and this verb serves to describe how the boundary line follows and runs along the Sea of Kinnereth (the Sea of Galilee). It is a very technical and geographical usage.
H4229B.portee: This word shows how God establishes clear and measured limits for His people. The boundaries are not arbitrary: they follow the natural markers (seas, rivers, mountains) that God has created. For the believer, this teaches that God's will is inscribed in creation and respects the order He has put in place.

sens: That contains a lot of marrow
Rich, flavorful, nourishing (referring to food)
That has substance, strength (in a figurative sense)
H4229C.detail: 1. The word primarily designates what is filled with marrow — this fatty and nutritious substance that fills the interior of bones. In Isaiah 25:6, the prophet speaks of dishes "full of marrow" to describe the savory and richly nourishing food that the Lord prepares for the peoples in the coming times. 2. By extension, "full of marrow" expresses the idea of richness and abundance in food, which truly nourishes the body. It is a feast of quality, not bland or meager food. 3. Figuratively, this term evokes what has substance, vital strength, that which supports and fortifies — an image of divine generosity toward those who belong to Him.
H4229C.origine: The Hebrew word mâchâh comes from a root that expresses the idea of filling or being fat. The marrow of bones was renowned for its nutritional value and energy abundance in biblical thought, symbolizing wealth and life. The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 25:6, making its use in this context of eschatological blessing all the more remarkable.
H4229C.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 25:6, in a magnificent prophecy announcing the messianic feast that the Lord prepares for all peoples on the holy mountain. In this passage, the dishes "full of marrow" evoke not only abundant and rich food but also divine excellence and generosity toward the nations. It is a picture of complete satisfaction and forthcoming blessing.
H4229C.portee: For the believer, this image of the feast filled with dishes full of marrow speaks of the deep satisfaction that only God can provide — not a superficial satisfaction, but something nourishing, substantial, that truly supports the soul. It promises that those who cling to God will receive not just the bare necessities, but overflowing generosity. It invites the reader to seek in the Lord, rather than in the things of the world, the wealth that truly satisfies.

sens: Geometric instrument used to draw circles or to transfer distances
Tool of the carpenter or draftsman for marking contours and proportions
H4230.detail: 1. The compass is an instrument with two articulated arms: one pointed (the sharp point), the other equipped with a pencil or blade. It is used to draw perfect circles on a surface — a fundamental gesture of geometry. The Hebrew word literally means "that which draws a circle." 2. In Isaiah 44:13, the carpenter "marks" the dimensions of an idol with the compass: he uses it to transfer measurements, draw the shapes of the body, and ensure that the proportions are harmonious. It is the tool for precise drawing, allowing the human creator to give a regular and beautiful shape to his work.
H4230.origine: The Hebrew word מְחוּגָה comes from the root חוּג (houag), which means "to make a circle" or "to form a curve." This root evokes the action of tracing or delimiting in an arc. The compass is thus named after its primary function: it is "that which makes circles." The same root appears in other biblical contexts to denote circular movements or enclosed spaces.
H4230.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 44:13. In this passage, the prophet ironically describes the process of making a wooden idol: the carpenter successively uses the cord, the pencil, the knife, and the compass to shape his work. The compass symbolizes the search for regular and beautiful proportions — but in the service of a false deity. The prophet wants to show that despite all his skill and tools, man remains incapable of creating true life or transcendent power.
H4230.portee: This passage in Isaiah highlights the limits of human genius: even equipped with the best instruments, even capable of perfect mathematical proportions, man can only create inert forms. For the reader, it is a call to recognize that only God is the creator of true life, and that idols — however beautiful they may be — are merely shaped wood, without power or substance. The compass thus becomes a symbol of human technique separated from God.

sens: Natural or constructed harbor where ships find shelter
Safe refuge, desired destination
H4231.detail: 1. A port is a haven where ships can anchor and find protection. It is a place of safety on the water, either constructed or naturally favorable. In Psalms 107:30, after a storm is calmed, the Lord leads the sailors "to their desired port" — that is, to their destination, to the safe place they wanted to reach. 2. By extension, the word evokes any arrival at a safe harbor, any expected refuge after an ordeal. The port symbolizes here salvation and divine protection: God calms the storm and leads His servants to the haven they hoped for.
H4231.origine: The Hebrew word maḥoz literally means "province" or "district," but it is also used to refer to a port or coast — probably linked to the image of geographical boundaries, a defined place. In Hebrew, it appears rarely; its only biblical use in the sense of port is found in Psalm 107, where it conveys the idea of a safe and desired destination.
H4231.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 107:30. This psalm celebrates the deliverance of the Lord: after describing a terrifying storm that shakes the sailors, the psalmist recounts how God calms the waves and leads them to their desired port. This context clearly establishes that the port is the expected goal, the haven of peace and safety.
H4231.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian life experiences storms — trials, periods of trouble — but that God is the one who calms the waves and guides His children to the haven of safety and peace. It encourages the believer to trust in the protection and guidance of the Lord, even in the midst of distress.

sens: Antediluvian man, son of Irad and father of Metushelach
H4232.detail: Mehujaël is a man who lived before the Flood, belonging to the genealogical line of Cain. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 4:18, where he appears in the succession of generations: his father is Irad and his son is Metushelach. This name means "smitten by God," possibly evoking an action of God in his life or that of his family.
H4232.origine: The name Mehujaël combines two Hebrew elements: a root suggesting the idea of being "struck" or "touched" and the divine name God (El in Hebrew). The overall meaning points to an intervention or divine action. This character is situated in the pre-flood genealogy of Cain, before Noah and his family were saved during the Flood.
H4232.emploi: Mehujaël appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 4:18. He is listed in the long genealogy descending from Cain and shows the succession of human generations before the Flood. This list also includes Enoch (who was taken to heaven according to Genesis 5), and it continues to Lamech, the father of Noah. Mehujaël himself is not the subject of any particular action reported: he is simply named to establish the familial link between Irad and Metushelach.

sens: People or clan from which Eliel, one of David's warriors, originated
H4233.detail: Machavim apparently designates a locality or clan from which Eliel, a mighty warrior in the service of King David, came. This is the only place in the Bible where this name appears (1 Chronicles 11:46), in the list of the "mighty men" who supported David. Little is known about it: it was notable enough to mark the origin of a high-ranking fighter, but the place itself is not described elsewhere.
H4233.origine: The Hebrew name מַחֲוִים (Machavim) may derive from a root evoking propagation or growth, or it may simply correspond to a toponym (place name) whose etymology escapes us. It is a very local name, rarely attested in biblical sources.
H4233.emploi: Machavim appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:46.
