H4270.emploi: This word appears thirteen times in the Old Testament, mainly in Proverbs and in a few legislative and poetic passages. In the laws of compassion (Deuteronomy 15:8), it denotes the concrete needs of the poor that must be addressed. In the Psalms and Proverbs, lack is often presented as a consequence of behavior: restlessness leads to famine (Proverbs 21:5), while the Lord provides for the needs of those who fear him (Psalms 34:10). Generosity enriches, while greed impoverishes (Proverbs 11:24). The word thus covers both the objective state of poverty and the moral lesson that biblical wisdom draws from it.
H4270.portee: This word reminds the believer that poverty exists and that helping the poor is a moral duty: God calls everyone not to close their hand. But it also teaches that lack is not a fatality: it can be avoided through honesty, work, and generosity, and above all, that those who fear the Lord will lack nothing. It is an invitation both to practical mercy and to trust in divine providence.

sens: Grandfather of Baruch, scribe of Jeremiah
H4271.detail: Machséja is a man from the time of the divided monarchy, mentioned twice in the book of Jeremiah. He is the grandfather of Baruch, the faithful scribe and friend of the prophet Jeremiah. His name means "the Lord is a refuge" or "the Lord is a protection." He appears in the genealogy of Baruch (Jeremiah 32:12) and in that of Serajah (Jeremiah 51:59), who was the chief chamberlain to King Zedekiah and who carried Jeremiah's scroll to Babylon.
H4271.origine: The name Machséja means "Jehovah is a refuge" (or "shelter"). It combines the divine name with the idea of protection, security. This theophoric name expresses trust in God as a protector, characteristic of pious Hebrew names of the time.
H4271.emploi: Machséja is mentioned twice in the book of Jeremiah, during the Babylonian captivity. In Jeremiah 32:12, he is identified as the father of Neriah and the grandfather of Baruch, the scribe of Jeremiah who received and kept the prophet's words. In Jeremiah 51:59, the same Neriah (son of Machséja) is presented as the father of Serajah, chief chamberlain of King Zedekiah, who was tasked with carrying the prophetic scroll to Babylon. Machséja thus belongs to a family of dignitaries and figures close to the prophet during the last days of Judah before the exile.

sens: Strike with force to shatter, reduce to pieces
Severely injure, deliver a destructive blow
Defeat, annihilate an opponent in battle
Dominate, render powerless
H4272.detail: 1. The most concrete meaning of the verb is to strike something with such violence that it breaks, shattering it into fragments. It conveys the idea of physical destruction: "I annihilate them, I break them, and they do not rise again" (2 Samuel 22:39). 2. The word also applies to severely injuring a person or an animal. God says: "I wound and I heal" (Deuteronomy 32:39), showing that this word describes a deep bodily injury, not a scratch. 3. In images of battle and divine power, breaking expresses total victory: "God will break the heads of his enemies" (Psalms 68:22), or "the Lord breaks kings in the day of his anger" (Psalms 110:5). It is to crush an opponent, rendering them incapable of rising. 4. The verb also describes the action of mastering and reducing to nothing. When God "breaks the pride" of the sea (Job 26:12), it is not about shattering the water, but taming its wild force, submitting it to his authority.
H4272.origine: The Hebrew verb מָחַץ comes from a root that evokes a violent blow, a destructive impact. The family of the word includes terms related to striking, to hitting, to reducing to dust. The basic image is that of a warrior striking his enemy with such force that the weapon or blow passes through, causing a deep and mortal wound, or that of something breaking under a violent impact.
H4272.emploi: The verb appears about fourteen times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Deuteronomy, and historical narratives. It is very often used to describe God's warrior action: he breaks enemies, pulverizes kings, crushes those who stand against him and his people. It is also found in contexts where God manifests his power over creation — he breaks the pride of the sea (Job 26:12) — or in promises of punishment. The word can sometimes be used in the sense of injuring rather than killing, as in the phrase "I wound and I heal" (Deuteronomy 32:39), where it expresses divine authority over life and death, sickness and healing.
H4272.portee: This verb reveals that the God of the Bible is not an abstract and distant power: he acts concretely in history, he fights for his people, he breaks the power of his enemies. For the believer, this reminds us that God has the power to overcome all that opposes his plan, and that no human force can ultimately resist him. It is a word of comfort for those who live under the weight of oppression or threat: God is never indifferent, he intervenes, and his victory is certain.

sens: serious injury caused by a blow
contusion with deep lesion
moral or spiritual harm or damage
H4273.detail:
1. A wound is a serious injury caused by a violent impact, a blow that tears or bruises the skin and tissues. In Isaiah 30:26, it refers to the injury inflicted on the people by their oppressors or their distance from God: "the Lord will bind up the wound of His people, and He will heal the wound of their blows."
2. It is a deep contusion, a lesion that does not heal easily and bears the mark of the violence suffered. The Hebrew word evokes the image of a bleeding wound that requires care and time to heal.
3. Figuratively, it refers to anything that wounds the soul or spirit of a people: collective suffering, trauma, rupture with God. In the context of Isaiah, it is the restoration after divine judgment.
H4273.origine: The Hebrew word מַחַץ (machats) comes from a root meaning to strike, to hit hard, to reach with violence. It describes the blow itself and especially its consequence: the wound. It is found in contexts where violence causes a lasting lesion.
H4273.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 30:26. It describes the spiritual and physical wound of the people of Israel, bruised by wars and exile. The prophet Isaiah announces that the Lord will heal this wound: the promise is not only medical but restorative. God not only bandages the wound, He erases the scar and restores the people to their fullness.
H4273.portee: This verse invites the reader to meditate on divine healing: God does not merely bandage the wounds of His people, He heals them completely. For the Christian, it is a promise of restoration and renewal after the wounds of life. The wound becomes the place where the compassion and healing power of the Lord are manifested.

sens: Stone extracted and worked for construction
Masonry material worked and ready for use
Expenses or materials necessary for repairs
H4274.detail:
1. A hewn stone is a stone extracted from a quarry and then shaped, dressed, and cut by workers to fit together regularly in a construction. It is quality material, prepared and finished, unlike raw stone. The three biblical passages mention these hewn stones in the repairs of the temple in Jerusalem (2 Kings 12:12, 2 Kings 22:6, 2 Chronicles 34:11), always purchased among other construction materials: wood, framing, cut elements ready for use.
2. The word also refers, by extension, to the work of hewing itself — the action of dressing, shaping the stone. It is the effort of the craftsmen that makes the stone usable.
3. Specifically, in the three biblical contexts, "hewn stones" appears in a list of material expenses: money is used to buy these prepared stones, wood, framing, and other needs for repairing or restoring the temple. The word here designates the essential material.
H4274.origine: The Hebrew word מַחְצֵב (machtsev) comes from the root חצב (chatsav), which means "to cut, to carve, to hew" — initially with an axe or chisel. This root evokes the action of transforming raw material into a worked object. Other words from the same family express the work of hewing: the verb וַיַּחְצֹב "and he hewed" describes the workers who sculpt or shape. The name machtsev thus carries the idea of a stone that has undergone this transformation.
H4274.emploi: The word appears only three times in biblical Hebrew, all three passages concerning the repairs of the temple in Jerusalem (2 Kings 12, 2 Kings 22, and 2 Chronicles 34). In each case, it appears in a list of purchased materials: hewn stones, wood, framing. The context shows that these stones are prepared and costly material, distinct from raw stone, purchased from suppliers or stonecutters. The meaning is consistent: quality construction material, cut and ready for use.
H4274.portee: This word reminds us that the service of God — here, the maintenance and restoration of His temple — requires planning, investment, and skilled labor. The hewn stones symbolize the raw material transformed, refined, made suitable to be joined with others in a lasting construction. For the believer, this evokes the idea that God cares for practical details and that His work is built stone by stone, with care and solidity.

sens: Division of a whole into two equal parts
One of the two parts obtained after division
In the context of spoils or sharing, the portion that belongs to a person or group
H4275.detail:
1. The word denotes a division into two equal parts: it is half in the mathematical sense of the term. When something is divided by two, you obtain a half (Numbers 31:36-43).
2. It also refers to one of the two parts resulting from such a division. In the sharing of the spoils of war against Midian, the soldiers receive their share, which the text calls the "half," just as the assembly of Israel receives its share.
3. The word is used to designate the portion or share that legally belongs to someone in a division: it is the quota that comes to you. The two groups (warriors and people) each receive an equal "share" of the captured spoils.
H4275.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to cut" or "to divide." A half is literally what results when you cut or divide a whole into two. This idea of cutting, of separation into two parts, is at the heart of the meaning of the word.
H4275.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Numbers 31:36 and 31:43. These two occurrences concern the sharing of the captured spoils during the victory over Midian. On one side, the half goes to the warriors who fought (verse 36); on the other, the half is allocated to the assembly of Israel that remained in the camp (verse 43). In both cases, the word "half" or "share" designates an equal portion of the spoils: three hundred thirty-seven thousand five hundred sheep. The context shows that the sharing respects a principle of equality, each group receiving its fair share.
H4275.portee: This passage reminds us of an important biblical principle: the fair sharing of the fruit of labor and victory. Even in a context of war, God commands that the spoils be divided equitably between those who fought and the entire community. This teaches that blessings and resources should not enrich some at the expense of others, but be distributed justly.

sens: Division of a whole into two equal parts
One of the two equal parts of a whole
Half-quantity in a measure or weight
Midday, noon
H4276.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to the division of a whole into two equal parts. In Exodus 30:23, half of myrrh is taken to prepare the holy anointing oil: 250 shekels out of 500, exactly the division in two. 2. It then refers to one of the two parts obtained from this division. In Numbers 31:30, it speaks of the half of the goods that goes to the children of Israel, as opposed to the other half reserved for the warriors. 3. The word is also used for half-measures or half-weights used in transactions. In Exodus 30:13, each must give half a shekel, that is, half of the standard weight of the sanctuary (20 gerahs instead of 40). 4. Rarely, it denotes the middle of the day, the moment of noon when the sun is at its highest. This meaning is less common in the provided usages, but it comes from the idea of "middle."
H4276.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to divide" or "to split." The form with the prefix ma- indicates that we are talking about half as a concrete reality, something that can be counted and measured. It is a term from everyday life, used in commerce, liturgy, and administration to speak of shares, portions, and weights.
H4276.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Bible, mainly in legislative and administrative passages. It is frequently found in the book of Exodus, where it regulates the collection of the half-shekel for the sanctuary (Exodus 30:13-15, 38:26), and in Leviticus for daily offerings (Leviticus 6:13, where the sacrifice is divided between morning and evening). The books of Numbers use this word to distribute the war booty between the fighters and the people (Numbers 31:29-30, 31:42, 31:47). It also appears in military and administrative contexts in 1 Kings and 1 Chronicles. The meaning remains always precise and concrete: it is about dividing equitably or measuring a determined share.
H4276.portee: This word reminds the believer that God ordains equity and justice in the sharing of goods and responsibilities. The laws regarding the half-share of the sanctuary and the war booty show that even wealth and the fruits of labor must be distributed according to divine wisdom, never arbitrarily. For the modern reader, it is an invitation to reflect on fair and equitable sharing.

sens: To break or pierce by driving in a pointed or sharp object
To completely destroy, annihilate
H4277.detail:
1. To split primarily means to break or pierce a solid object by striking it forcefully, especially with a pointed tool or a violent blow. The only biblical usage shows Jael driving a tent peg into Sisera's head: "She struck Sisera, split his head, crushed and pierced his temple" (Judges 5:26). It is a brutal and definitive action that destroys the victim.
2. The broader meaning of the Hebrew verb is to completely destroy, annihilate. This verb expresses total, irreversible destruction—not just damaging, but reducing to nothing.
H4277.origine: The Hebrew verb מָחַק (machaq) evokes the image of driving in, breaking by a violent blow. Its root carries the idea of complete and irreversible destruction. The word belongs to a family of Hebrew terms expressing ruin and total annihilation of a person or reality.
H4277.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Judges 5:26, in the Song of Deborah which celebrates Israel's victory over Sisera. Jael, a foreign woman, kills the sleeping enemy general by driving a tent peg into his head. This warrior and violent context concentrates all the force of the verb: it is a sudden and total destruction of an enemy. The uniqueness of this usage makes it a rare word, but its narrative and poetic impact is considerable.
H4277.portee: This account shows how God can use humble and unexpected people to accomplish His purposes. Jael, a woman and a foreigner, becomes the instrument of Israel's victory. Her violent act reminds us that divine justice can sometimes be exercised through dramatic means, and that faithfulness to God can take surprising forms depending on the circumstances of life.

sens: The extent or space that extends downward, particularly the hidden interior of the earth
The inner, hidden, or inaccessible domain
What is far from the surface or sight
H4278.detail: 1. Depth refers to the space that sinks below the surface of the earth. In Psalm 95:4, God "holds the depths of the earth in His hand": the image evokes these secret cavities, the bowels of the earth that only the Creator can explore and possess. 2. The word can also refer to what is hidden, distant, impenetrable to the ordinary man. That is why it is associated with what escapes the eye: the abysses, the underground spaces that belong to God alone. 3. Figuratively, any hidden, inaccessible, or mysterious region can be called a depth.
H4278.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of traversing, crossing a space. The primary image is that of an expanse being explored, a path or field being searched. The name carries the idea of a zone that is difficult to access, deep, requiring investigation.
H4278.emploi: This word appears only once in the preserved Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 95:4. The Bible uses it to express that God controls the hidden regions of creation, inaccessible to man. It is a poetic term, mainly used in hymns of praise to magnify divine power over the entire universe.
H4278.portee: Psalm 95 invites the reader to recognize God's absolute sovereignty, who is not only King of the visible heights but master of buried secrets. Meditating on this verse strengthens trust: God reigns not only over what we see but also over all that escapes us and frightens us.

sens: The day following the present day
An unspecified or distant future moment
The future, the time to come
H4279.detail:
1. The day following the present day: this is the most literal and common meaning. When Jonathan says to David, "Tomorrow is the new moon" (1 Samuel 20:18), he is referring to the very next day, the exact day that comes after today. Similarly, Moses announces to the people, "Tomorrow is the day of rest, the Sabbath" (Exodus 16:23), specifically designating the following day.
2. An unspecified or distant future moment: the word broadens to refer to any moment that is not now, without specifying how much time will pass. When King Jehu orders, "Come to me tomorrow at this time" (2 Kings 10:6), it may indicate a set delay for action but not immediate. This is also how promises or realities that will only manifest later are spoken of.
3. The future, the time to come: in more philosophical or wisdom literature passages, "tomorrow" evokes everything that is to come, that which is not yet. The wise say, "Do not say to your neighbor, 'Go, and come back; tomorrow I will give'" (Proverbs 3:28) to show the uncertainty of any future. It is the idea that the future is never guaranteed and remains in God's hands.
H4279.origine: The Hebrew word מָחָר comes from a root that expresses the idea of "that which comes after," "that which follows." Its exact etymology is not absolutely certain, but the image is clear: it is the time that unfolds before oneself, after the present. In Hebrew, this same word is used in all temporal contexts to speak of what is to come, from tomorrow to the more distant future. It is a very ancient and fundamental word for expressing the relationship of the people of Israel to time and divine providence.
H4279.emploi: This word appears 52 times in the Hebrew Bible, initially very concentrated in the Pentateuch and historical books, less so in the poetic ones. It is used to set precise appointments: Jonathan informs David of his presence at the new moon tomorrow, Jehu gives a deadline for action by tomorrow noon. It also introduces acts of God: Joshua announces to the people that "tomorrow the Lord will do wonders" (Joshua 3:5), Moses that "tomorrow" will be the Sabbath rest. Finally, it appears in warnings and promises: the Lord tells Pharaoh what will happen tomorrow (the plagues), and the proverbs warn against those who constantly put things off until tomorrow. The word emphasizes the limit of our knowledge of the future and our dependence on God.
H4279.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on their relationship to time. The Bible uses it to show that the future belongs solely to God, not to us: we do not know what tomorrow will bring. It is a call to vigilance (do not put off until tomorrow what you must do today), to faith (God also masters what is to come), and to trust (even the wonders of tomorrow are in the Lord's hands). The word brings us back to our smallness and finitude in the face of divine sovereignty.

sens: The sharp blade of a plow that breaks the ground
Agricultural tool used for tilling the soil
H4281.detail: 1. The share is the sharp, metallic part of a plow, the one that penetrates the soil and breaks it to prepare for tilling. It is the active element of the instrument: in 1 Samuel 13:20, it is mentioned among the tools of Israelite farmers that must be sharpened by the Philistines, alongside the hoe and the axe. 2. More broadly, it is one of the essential tools of agricultural work, used for cultivating the land. When the blade becomes dull, as recalled in 1 Samuel 13:21, it must be straightened or sharpened to remain effective. The wear of the share testifies to the constant labor of the farmer.
H4281.origine: The Hebrew word מַחֲרֵשָׁה (ma-cha-ré-shah) derives from a root meaning "to till" or "to dig." It literally designates that which plows, the instrument of tilling. It is a feminine noun formed from the verb חָרַשׁ (cha-rash), "to till the earth." The word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of ancient agriculture.
H4281.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Samuel 13, during an episode where the Israelites are under Philistine domination. The Philistines monopolize metallurgy and force the Israelites to go down to them to sharpen their agricultural tools, including the shares. This episode illustrates the technological advantage of the Philistines: they control metalworking, while the Israelites depend on them to maintain their instruments. The share always appears alongside other tools for tilling or combat (hoe, axe, trident), which underscores its importance in daily life.
H4281.portee: This passage reminds us that even the most ordinary occupations — tilling the land — depend on the political context and access to technology. It also shows that the life of the farmer, inscribed in the natural cycles of agricultural work, remains vulnerable to the power dynamics between peoples. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to reflect on God's providence in the details of life and on true riches: not technical domination, but faithfulness to God.

sens: The day that immediately follows the present day
The morning of a new day
The moment that follows an event, marking a turning point
H4283.detail:
1. The day that immediately follows the present day — this is the simplest and most common meaning of the word. When an event occurs, it is said to happen or be observed "the next day." For example, in Genesis 19:34, Lot's older daughter says to her sister, "I lay with my father last night; let us make him drink wine again tonight," which shows that "the next day" is the following day when one can act differently. Similarly, in 1 Samuel 31:8, "the next day," the Philistines came to strip the dead, marking the continuation of events from the battle.
2. The morning of a new day — the word sometimes designates the starting point of the following day, especially when emphasizing awakening and renewal. In 1 Samuel 5:4, "the next day, having risen early in the morning," the people discover that Dagon has been overturned: it is the morning that follows the night that has passed. In Numbers 11:32, the people gathered quails "the next day" after they had fallen in abundance.
3. The moment that follows an event, marking a turning point — in contexts where the word expresses the decisive moment that changes the situation. In Joshua 5:12, the manna ceased "the next day" after Passover: this is the moment when God changes the diet for His people, marking their entry into Canaan. In Leviticus 7:16, the meat of the sacrifice must be eaten on the day it is offered, and "what remains shall be eaten the next day": this is a limit that regulates the order of worship.
H4283.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of turning, changing direction — hence naturally the idea of the following day, the one towards which one turns. The word is formed with a prefix indicating state or position (prefix "m") and the root "hr" meaning "after" or "following." In the Greek Old Testament, this word may correspond to Greek terms also expressing the day or the morning that follows.
H4283.emploi: The word appears 32 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives and legal texts. It is used to mark the progression of events: battles (1 Samuel 31:8), appearances of signs (1 Samuel 5:4), cultic instructions (Leviticus 7:16), movements of the people (Numbers 11:32). Sometimes it marks a legal limit (Leviticus 23:11), or simply the continuity of an action (Exodus 18:13). The word is neutral, purely chronological: it carries no emotional weight but situates the event in time to clarify its order and succession.
H4283.portee: This simple word reminds us that in the Bible, time is important: God acts in history in days and nights, not in the abstract. Each day counts, and "the next day" often marks a moment when God renews His action or when the people discover the consequences of the previous day. It is an invitation to live the Christian life day by day, waiting for what the Lord will do "the next day," just as our ancestors had to live by faith one day at a time.

sens: What occupies the mind, what one thinks
Plan formed in the heart to act
Project that one meditates on, design
Ability to imagine and conceive a work
Hidden intention, plot
H4284.detail:
1. Thought is primarily what crosses the mind and heart of man. In Genesis 6:5, the thoughts of men were only toward evil: these are the intimate movements of their heart, what they ruminated deep within themselves. In Proverbs 15:26, evil thoughts are an abomination to the Lord: this word designates the moral stream of reflection of a person.
2. A thought becomes a project when it is engraved in one’s heart to realize it. In Jeremiah 29:11, the Lord says: "For I know the plans I have for you, plans for peace" — it is a settled plan, a resolution. In Proverbs 20:18, "the plan is established by counsel": it speaks of an intention that one prepares thoughtfully.
3. Sometimes, the word designates a true plot or a hidden intention to do harm. In Jeremiah 11:19, the enemies of the prophet "think against him": it is a conspiratorial thought, a design against someone. In Lamentations 3:60, Jeremiah cries: "You have seen all their vengeance, all their plans against me": plans of malice.
4. A thought can also be a creation of the mind, an inventive skill. In 2 Chronicles 2:14, Huram-Abi is skilled "in all kinds of sculptures and artistic objects": here, the word designates art, that is to say, creative thought brought into form.
H4284.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to count, calculate, estimate". It is related to the idea of weighing something in one’s mind, turning it over in one’s heart. Thought is what stirs within us and what we "count" or "weigh". The Greek translates this word as "logismós" (calculation) or "diánoia" (intention of the mind), terms that retain this image of reflective thinking.
H4284.emploi: This word appears 52 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Isaiah. It can simply designate an ordinary thought of the heart (Genesis 6:5, Proverbs 15:26), but also a great divine project — the thoughts of the Lord that endure forever (Psalms 33:11, Jeremiah 29:11). It also describes the thoughts and plans of men, often to show how they fail in the face of God’s designs (Proverbs 19:21, Isaiah 55:8-9). In contexts of tension or conflict, it takes on a darker meaning: evil thoughts, plots (Jeremiah 11:19, Lamentations 3:60). Finally, it can mean know-how, artistic invention (2 Chronicles 2:14).
H4284.portee: This word reminds us that God knows our most secret and intimate thoughts — which should lead us to guard our hearts. It also shows that human projects, even intelligent ones, remain subject to God’s eternal designs: as Jeremiah 29:11 says, His plans for us are "plans for peace". For the Christian, it is an invitation to abandon one’s own thoughts and to accept that God sees and governs what happens in our hearts.

sens: the absence of light, obscurity
a dark, hidden, or remote place
the hiding place, secrecy
the grave, the abode of the dead
H4285.detail:
1. Darkness primarily refers to physical obscurity, the absence of light — what one can see or imagine when there is nothing to illuminate. This is why Isaiah 42:16 speaks of turning darkness into light to guide the blind on an unknown path.
2. The word also designates a dark or remote place, a location that is not well seen: the "dark places of the land" in Psalms 74:20 evoke the hidden lairs of robbers, places where darkness and disorder reign.
3. It also signifies secrecy, what is hidden or concealed — notably the shameful actions one wants to hide from view: Isaiah 29:15 denounces those who "do their works in darkness", that is to say, in secret, out of sight.
4. Finally, darkness evokes the grave and the world of the dead, this dark realm from which one does not return: Psalms 88:7 and 143:3 associate darkness with the deep pit and the dwelling of the deceased, a place of extreme distress.
H4285.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of blackening, obscuring, covering. It is from the same family as the verb "to be dark" or "to make dark". In Aramaic, the equivalent form is "chashokh", with the same meaning of obscurity. This term belongs to the basic vocabulary of the Bible to describe darkness, both in the literal sense and in the figurative sense of what is hidden or evil.
H4285.emploi: This word appears about 7 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and in Isaiah. It is used both in the concrete sense (the physical darkness of a place) and in the figurative sense (secrecy, concealment, death). In the lament psalms, such as Psalms 88 and 143, the psalmist uses darkness to express his extreme distress and his feeling of being trapped in a hopeless world. In the oracles of Isaiah, particularly in 29:15 and 42:16, the word symbolizes either human malice (hidden acts) or the desperate situation of the people that God promises to transform. The context determines whether it should be understood as an image of death, shameful secrets, or physical obscurity.
H4285.portee: This word reminds the reader that nothing is truly hidden from God: the darkness in which some think they work in secret is only light to the Lord. But it also reminds us that God has the power to transform the thickest darkness — whether physical, moral, or existential — into light. It is a word of hope as much as a warning: hope for those who are going through darkness, warning for those who believe they can hide their actions.

sens: Action of stripping something of what covers it
Removal of the bark from a branch or wood
H4286.detail:
1. The word designates the action of exposing, revealing what was hidden or covered. It is the gesture of someone who removes a protective or aesthetic layer. In Genesis 30:37, Jacob peels the bark from the branches of poplar, almond, and plane, revealing the white wood underneath: he literally uncovers the white of the branches.
2. More specifically, it is the removal of the bark, this natural envelope that protects and colors the wood. This simple yet intentional gesture transforms the appearance of the wood by making its internal structure visible.
H4286.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be bare, uncovered". It expresses the idea of exposure, of removing a veil or garment. The underlying root evokes the contrast between what hides and what is revealed.
H4286.emploi: This term appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 30:37. Jacob uses it during a crafty shepherding action: he peels branches to make them speckled, then places them before the flocks to influence their breeding. It is a concrete detail of the patriarchal narrative, without major theological significance, but illustrating Jacob's ingenuity.
H4286.portee: This word reminds us that even small gestures of daily life — here, an agricultural or pastoral act — can serve human purposes. It does not carry spiritual weight but shows how the Bible notes the concrete details of the ordinary life of the patriarchs.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Korah, son of Amasaï
Assistant to King Hezekiah for the purification of the temple
H4287G.detail: 1. Machath is a Levite from the house of Korah, meaning he is a descendant of the priests and musicians of the tribe of Levi who served in the temple of Israel. His father is Amasaï. 2. Machath appears during the time of King Hezekiah, in the period of the divided monarchy, when this king undertakes to purify and restore the temple in Jerusalem. He is among the Levites chosen for this great religious work (2 Chronicles 29:12).
H4287G.origine: The Hebrew name Machath literally means "to seize" or "to grasp," evoking the idea of taking or holding firmly. This name is fitting for a man called to responsibilities in the service of the temple, a task requiring commitment and firmness.
H4287G.emploi: Machath appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 29:12. He is mentioned as one of the Levites from the house of Korah who rises to respond to the call of King Hezekiah. The context shows a major mobilization: the king gathers the priests and Levites to consecrate the temple anew and cleanse the holy places. Machath represents one of those faithful servants who accept this mission of spiritual restoration.
H4287G.portee: Machath embodies the role of the Levites as servants of worship and religious purification. His appearance in the account of Hezekiah's reform reminds the reader that the restoration of a nation's spiritual life comes through ordinary men who respond to the divine call and commit to the sanctification of the temple and the community.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi, from the family of Korah
H4287H.detail: Machath is a Levite belonging to the large family of Korah, a branch of the priestly tribe of Levi. He lived during the time of the divided kingdom, probably during the reign of King Hezekiah. His Hebrew name evokes the idea of "to seize" or "to take." Machath was responsible, under the leadership of Conania and his brother Shimeï, for managing the offerings and gifts destined for the temple of Jerusalem, alongside other Levites such as Jehiel, Azazia, and Benaja (2 Chronicles 31:13).
H4287H.origine: The name Machath comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to seize" or "to hold firmly." This name evokes the ability to take charge, to manage, to master — an appropriate image for a temple officer responsible for the reserves and offerings.
H4287H.emploi: Machath is mentioned only once in the entire Bible: in 2 Chronicles 31:13. He appears in the list of Levites that King Hezekiah had established to administer the revenues of the temple — the offerings, tithes, and dedicated gifts. He served under the authority of Conania and his brother Shimeï, as well as under that of the high priest Azariah. This single mention reveals a man holding a position of administration and trust in the temple during the great religious reform led by Hezekiah.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi, from the family of the Korahites
H4287I.detail: Machath is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi charged with the service of the tabernacle and the temple. He belongs to the family of the Korahites, an important branch of the Levites. His name appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Levi, in 1 Chronicles 6:35, where he is presented as the son of Amasaï and the father of Elkana, both also Levites. This genealogy shows how the responsibilities of worship were passed down from father to son in the priestly families.
H4287I.origine: The name Machath means "to seize" or "to take," evoking the action of grasping or holding firmly. It comes from a Hebrew root that carries this idea of taking or seizing. Machath is also another name for Ahimoth, as indicated by biblical tradition, and he is part of the long genealogical chain of the Levites of the temple.
H4287I.emploi: Machath appears in the genealogical records of the Levites during the time of the divided monarchy. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6:35 as a descendant of Korah (through the branch of Amasaï) and an ancestor of Elkana. This genealogy places Machath in the context of the regular Levitical service of the temple. His name reminds us of the importance of genealogical continuity and hereditary rights in the service of worship in Israel's tradition.

sens: Physical destruction, collapse of a structure
Loss of wealth, impoverishment
Annihilation, complete disappearance
State of fear or dread before a calamity
Inevitable and destructive consequence of an action
H4288.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the material destruction of a building or fortification: walls collapse, fortresses fall into ruins (Psalms 89:41).
2. In a broader sense, it signifies the loss of what one possesses, particularly wealth: poverty is a ruin for the destitute (Proverbs 10:15), just as the absence of people is a ruin for the prince (Proverbs 14:28).
3. The word also evokes total annihilation, what remains after destruction: it designates what has been broken and lies useless.
4. It can mean fear or dread in the face of danger: the terror of an impending disaster.
5. The Bible uses it to describe the inevitable consequence of bad actions: he who opens wide his lips is headed for ruin (Proverbs 13:3), the mouth of the fool is a near ruin (Proverbs 10:14), and the way of the wicked leads to ruin for those who follow it (Proverbs 10:29).
H4288.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to break" or "to strike," evoking the image of something broken into pieces. It is a name that describes the state of destruction and desolation that results. The Hebrew root suggests a violent rupture, a demolition rather than mere wear. The word appears in ancient texts to depict destroyed cities or razed fortifications.
H4288.emploi: This word appears eleven times in the Old Testament, mainly in Proverbs (seven occurrences) and in Psalms and the prophets. It primarily denotes the physical destruction of fortifications (Psalms 89:41). It then takes on an economic and social meaning: poverty ruins the destitute (Proverbs 10:15), the absence of people impoverishes the king (Proverbs 14:28). Biblical wisdom also uses it figuratively to warn against reckless words (Proverbs 10:14, 13:3), actions contrary to God's justice (Proverbs 10:29), and behaviors that lead to catastrophe. It is a word of consequence: it describes what awaits those who stray from God's path.
H4288.portee: This word reminds the believer that divine wisdom protects from ruin, while the fool rushes toward it. Proverbs uses it to show that our words, choices, and conduct have visible and lasting consequences. It is an invitation to prudence and obedience to God, who alone preserves from destruction.

sens: Portable metal container designed to hold fire or embers
Worship utensil used to offer incense before God
Tray or vessel intended to collect the ashes from the altar
H4289.detail:
1. A brazen altar is a metal container — typically made of gold or bronze depending on its purpose — designed to carry and maintain fire or embers. It is a practical and sturdy object that could be handled and filled with one hand (Numbers 16:17: "Each of you take your censer, put incense in it").
2. In Israel's worship, the brazen altar becomes a sacred instrument for presenting incense or offerings before the Lord. In Numbers 16:17-18, two hundred fifty men each bring their censer filled with incense during the judgment against Korah's rebellion. This ordinary object becomes a bearer of encounter with God.
3. The brazen altar also serves to collect the remnants from the altar: ashes and debris from sacrifices. In Exodus 27:3, ash pans are mentioned as altar utensils to maintain its cleanliness and proper function.
H4289.origine: The Hebrew word מַחְתָּה comes from a root expressing the idea of carrying or supporting something (hence its relation to the verb "to support"). It literally means "that which carries" or "that which supports" — here, what supports the fire. The same word indiscriminately designates the incense container, the brazen altar, or the ash pan: the essence is its function of holding and transporting. This term appears exclusively for objects of worship and the altar, never for ordinary containers.
H4289.emploi: The word appears 19 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in the books of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) and in the accounts of the Temple's construction (Kings, Chronicles). At the origins of the Tabernacle, the brazen altar is an indispensable utensil: they are counted on the altar of incense (Exodus 25:38), on the bronze altar (Exodus 27:3), and they are transported during relocations (Numbers 4:9). The religious use of the word becomes spectacular in Numbers 16, during Korah's illegal offering: each brings a censer of incense, and the censers of the rebels become a liturgical warning (Numbers 16:38: "With the censers of these men who have sinned... let them make broad plates to cover the altar"). The word retains the same objective meaning everywhere: it is always a container, never an abstraction.
H4289.portee: The brazen altar reminds the reader that worshiping God requires consecrated utensils and precise order. When Korah and his companions bring their censers without authorization, the fire from heaven consumes them (Numbers 16:35): the word becomes a witness to a sacred boundary that only the priests should cross. For the Christian, it also evokes that the encounter with God is never improvised — it follows ordered paths and a reverence of the heart.

sens: action of forcing entry into a place to steal
figuratively: violation, serious transgression of a law or order
H4290.detail:
1. Literally, it is the act of forcing a wall, door, or window to enter someone's property and steal. In Exodus 22:2, the law distinguishes the burglar caught in the act of breaking in (who can be killed without guilt) from the ordinary thief: there is an immediate, dangerous threat to life and property. The word evokes the noise and violence of one who breaks through a barrier.
2. Figuratively, in Jeremiah 2:34, God reproaches Judah not only for the blood of the innocents but for having shed it "without burglary" — that is, without the slightest trace of remorse or shame, in apparent impunity. The word becomes an image of the audacious violation of a moral law, a commandment, or a sacred order.
H4290.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to dig, to pierce." It concretely refers to the action of making a hole in a wall or obstacle to enter. The same family of words also describes the digging of a mine or piercing a barrier. This image of "forced digging" has naturally applied to any act of violation or illegitimate intrusion.
H4290.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 22:2, it is found in the civil law code: if a burglar who forces entry into a house at night is killed in the act, the owner does not incur the death penalty. In Jeremiah 2:34, the prophet uses it metaphorically: Judah has committed a crime against the innocents not secretly, but "without burglary," suggesting an ostentatious violence, insensitive to the consequences. In both cases, the word carries the idea of aggressive violation, not hidden theft.
H4290.portee: For the Christian reader, these two passages remind us that the Bible takes seriously the distinction between hidden crime and criminal insolence. In Exodus, it recognizes the right to self-defense against immediate danger. In Jeremiah, it condemns not only sin but especially the pride of one who sins without fear, as if he were above divine law. It is a lesson on judgment: God sees the heart that despises His will.

sens: To reach a place, to arrive there
To extend to (speaking of a thing)
To be realized, to be fulfilled (speaking of a word, a decree)
To arrive at (someone or something)
H4291.detail:
1. To reach a place or arrive there: the verb expresses the act of joining a goal, a destination. When Daniel interprets Nebuchadnezzar's dream, he speaks of the tree whose top rises "to the heavens" (Daniel 4:11), meaning it reaches that height.
2. To extend to: a material reality (like the top of a tree, the dominion of a king) touches, extends to a given point. The greatness of the king has "risen to the heavens" and his dominion "extends to the ends of the earth" (Daniel 4:22).
3. To be realized, to be fulfilled: when it concerns a decree or a word, the word means that it takes effect, that it materializes. The decree of the Most High "will be fulfilled" upon the king (Daniel 4:24), and indeed "all these things have been fulfilled" (Daniel 4:28).
4. To arrive at someone: to reach a person, to affect them, to happen to them. Before Daniel's accusers "reach" the bottom of the pit, the lions seize them (Daniel 6:24) — misfortune reaches them.
H4291.origine: The Aramaic word מְטָא (metâ) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to reach, to touch." Its image is that of movement that achieves, that arrives at its destination. This verb appears mainly in the prophetic and narrative passages of Daniel, books where Aramaic is spoken in the royal courts of Babylon and Persia.
H4291.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in biblical Aramaic, exclusively in the book of Daniel (4:11, 4:20, 4:22, 4:24, 4:28, 6:24, 7:13, 7:22). It is used both in a physical sense (the tree reaches the sky) and in a figurative or theological sense (a decree is fulfilled, a dominion extends, misfortune reaches someone). The context is almost always that of the fulfillment of divine will or the unfolding of royal events: interpretation of dreams, execution of judgments, or apocalyptic vision. Its meaning varies slightly depending on the subject, but the movement toward a term remains constant.
H4291.portee: This word teaches the reader that nothing remains in suspense: what God decrees reaches its fulfillment, what is spoken arrives at its destination. In the face of the powers of the world (Nebuchadnezzar, Darius), Daniel affirms that the decree of the Most High "will be fulfilled" — a word of faith and certainty. It is a call to trust: divine promises are never in vain, judgments are executed, and history goes where God leads it.

sens: tool for sweeping, made of twigs or fibers tied together
figuratively, instrument of destruction or annihilation
H4292.detail:
1. The broom is a cleaning tool made of twigs or fibers attached to a handle, used to sweep floors and remove dust and debris. It is a well-known everyday object for everyone.
2. In a figurative sense, the broom becomes an image of complete and radical destruction, of total eradication. When God says in Isaiah 14:23 that He will sweep Babylon "with the broom of destruction," He expresses that the city will be erased, annihilated without mercy, just as one sweeps away what is cluttering.
H4292.origine: The Hebrew word literally designates the sweeping tool. It comes from a root that evokes the act of sweeping or erasing. The image of the broom easily transitions from the concrete domain (cleaning a house) to the metaphorical domain (erasing a nation, a power).
H4292.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 14:23, in an oracle against Babylon. The prophet prophesies that God will reduce the great city to nothing and annihilate it. The use of the word "broom" reinforces the idea that Babylon, despite all its power and wealth, will be swept away like mere waste, treated with disregard, and will completely disappear. It is an image of vanity and the radical fall of human grandeur.
H4292.portee: This image of the divine broom reminds us that no human power, no matter how great, can withstand the will of God. Babylon, a feared empire, will be annihilated like dust. For the believer, this teaches the insignificance of the world's wealth and prestige: only what pleases God endures.

sens: Action of killing en masse, carnage
Place where animals are slaughtered
Figuratively: destruction, annihilation of a people or cause
H4293.detail:
1. The massacre is the act of killing many people or animals at once, a carnage. It is a brutal word that evokes death in large numbers, often with violence.
2. It is also the physical place where animals are slaughtered — what was once called a slaughterhouse or killing floor.
3. Figuratively, the Bible uses it to describe the complete annihilation of a people or the crushing of a human endeavor. In Isaiah 14:21, the prophet speaks of "preparing the massacre of the sons" to punish the iniquity of their fathers: it conveys the idea of total and inevitable destruction.
H4293.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to strike" or "to slaughter." It is formed from the verb טָבַח (tabach), which means to slaughter or kill. The same root gives rise to other words designating ritual slaughter or killing. It is a very concrete word, derived from the vocabulary of sacrifices and animal slaughter.
H4293.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 14:21. In this passage, the prophet Isaiah addresses a word against the king of Babylon and his pride. He announces that the tyrant's lineage will be destroyed: one must "prepare the massacre of the sons" so that they do not rise up to conquer the land. Here, the massacre is not an event that has already occurred, but something that God is preparing, a programmed destruction as punishment.
H4293.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's judgment on pride and iniquity is inevitable and terrible. It also shows that the sin of the fathers continues in the sons and calls for severe divine retribution. For the believer, it serves as a warning against trusting in one's own power and carnal designs.

sens: Stick or rigid stem held in hand
Branch or shoot of a plant
Symbol of authority of the leader of a tribe
Tribe of Israel, group of people organized under a leader
H4294G.detail:
1. The rod is primarily a simple and concrete object: a stick that one carries to walk, strike, or direct. Moses holds his rod in hand (Exodus 4:2), and it is with it that Aaron strikes the dust to create the lice of Egypt (Exodus 8:12) or that Moses brings forth water from the rock (Numbers 20:11). It is a daily tool, like the rod of Judah in Genesis 38:18.
2. In a botanical sense, the rod refers to a young branch or shoot of a plant, particularly of the vine. This sense is less frequent in the provided biblical usages, but it illuminates the image of a flexible and living stem.
3. The rod becomes a symbol of authority and power: Aaron's, kept before the testimony, represents the authority of the high priest (Numbers 17:10). The rod of the leader is the sign of his charge; thus, speaking of "twelve rods" in Numbers 17:2 refers to the leaders of the twelve tribes.
4. Finally, a tribe is the human group led by a chief who carries this rod: it is a "tribe of Israel," one of the twelve divisions of the people, originally organized around their respective princes.
H4294G.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of standing up, of being upright. The rod is literally what stands upright: a stick, a stem. This image of verticality and firmness has led it to symbolize authority (the one who holds the rod commands) and to designate the tribe as a structured human group. In Hebrew, the same word applies to a physical object and to a community, as both are organized, "erected."
H4294G.emploi: The word appears 46 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Pentateuch and the prophets. In miraculous contexts, the rod of Moses and Aaron is the instrument by which God performs the plagues of Egypt: it turns into a serpent (Exodus 7:10), strikes the waters and the dust. It symbolizes the divine power at work. In Numbers 17, Aaron's rod miraculously buds to testify to his legitimate priesthood, becoming a permanent sign of God's judgment. In the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah), the rod designates either the oppressor's staff that strikes Israel (Isaiah 9:3, 10:5) or a tool of correction and divine punishment. The sense of "tribe" is mainly administrative: the rods (the tribes) of Israel are counted according to the twelve sons of Jacob.
H4294G.portee: The rod teaches that true power is not in the object itself, but in the one who holds it and in the divine will it represents. Aaron's rod that buds affirms that God recognizes His servants and judges those who oppose Him. For the believer, it is a reminder that legitimate authority comes from God, and that He alone can transform a simple stick into an instrument of salvation or judgment. It is also an invitation to consider each tribe of Israel as a living reality, founded on the divine promise.

sens: Staff or rod serving as a symbol of power
Branch or vine shoot
Group of families sharing a common ancestry, led by a chief
H4294H.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a staff or rod, a symbol of a leader's authority: it is the physical object held in hand to exercise power (hence its unique literal use in Leviticus 24:11). 2. It also refers to a vine branch, a natural offshoot, as seen in biblical imagery where Israel is compared to a vine with its branches. 3. The main meaning in the Bible is that of tribe: a large group of families descending from a common ancestor (like the tribe of Judah, Ephraim, or Benjamin), always governed by a prince or chief. The twelve tribes of Israel form the entire people, and each occupies an assigned territory (Joshua 16:8, Numbers 34:23). The word evokes the original image of the leader holding his staff: the tribe is the community he leads and represents.
H4294H.origine: The Hebrew word matteh comes from a root meaning "to extend" or "to stretch out." Its original meaning is the staff or rod that is extended to strike or command. By natural extension, it designated the leader who holds this staff, and then the entire community under his authority. The tribe is thus like the staff: it has an elongated shape, a linear structure (counted by generations), and it obeys the leader who carries and directs it like one carries a staff.
H4294H.emploi: This word appears 149 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the Old Testament (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Joshua). It is omnipresent in the chapters of Numbers that organize the people around the Tabernacle: the princes of the twelve tribes (Numbers 1, 2, 7), the census of each tribe (Numbers 1:21-43), the allocation of Levitical cities by tribe (Numbers 35), the division of the promised land tribe by tribe (Numbers 34, Joshua 16). Each tribe corresponds to a prince, a territory, a responsibility. The word embodies the organization of God's people under the old covenant: a very clear genealogical and territorial structure.
H4294H.portee: Understanding the system of the twelve tribes helps the modern reader grasp the unity of the people of Israel in the Old Testament: despite their differences, they form one body united by a common ancestry and by the covenant with God. The tribes remind us that God cares about order, structure, and collective responsibility: each has its place, its role, its heritage. For the Christian, this foreshadows the Church as the body of Christ with many distinct members but united under one head.

sens: Arrow or projectile shot from a bow
Word, message, or judgment sent by God against His enemies
H4294I.detail:
1. An arrow is primarily a projectile, the sharp object shot from a bow. It is the fastest and most piercing weapon in battle: it flies straight toward its target and pierces it. In Habakkuk 3:9, God's "arrows" are the fearsome arrows of His judgment, deployed against the enemies of Israel.
2. By extension, the word designates anything that strikes like an arrow: the words of God Himself. In Habakkuk 3:14, God "pierces with His arrows" the enemy leaders, meaning that His words of judgment hit them squarely, with the same destructive power as a volley of arrows. The arrow becomes the image of the divine word that judges, wounds, and destroys what opposes God.
H4294I.origine: The Hebrew word מַטֶּה comes from a root that first evokes the staff, the stem, then the branch, and finally the tribe (an organized group like a stem with its members). Here, in the provided usages, the meaning "arrow" comes from the image of the pointed and elongated trait like a slender branch. It is a very concrete word, derived from the vocabulary of weapons and staffs.
H4294I.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, and both occurrences are found in Habakkuk 3, the magnificent victory song of the prophet. In verses 9 and 14, the context is that of the theophany — the appearance of God in glory to fight the enemies of His people. The "arrows" in question are the arrows of divine wrath, instruments of judgment and destruction. The word transposes the usual warrior imagery to the supernatural power of God: His words and judgments are as fearsome and inevitable as arrows shot with full force. This poetic language emphasizes the certainty and irresistibility of divine judgment.
H4294I.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the power of God's word. Just as an arrow cannot miss its target, the divine word unfailingly reaches its goal: it judges, it saves, it transforms. For the one who receives it, it can be either the arrow of salvation or the arrow of judgment. This image also reminds us of the energy with which God acts in history: nothing can stop His plans.

sens: Wooden object used to strike or to advance
Branch of a tree or plant
Subdivision of a people, group led by a chief
H4294J.detail:
1. The oldest and most concrete meaning: a stick, a rod, or a staff used for striking, beating, or rubbing. Isaiah 28:27 clearly mentions this when grains are beaten with a stick.
2. By extension, a branch of a tree or vine, a woody shoot that naturally grows from a trunk. Ezekiel 19:11-12 describes the vine with its vigorous branches, and the fire that consumes these branches.
3. In a figurative and social sense, a branch becomes a tribe or clan: a group of people united by blood or loyalty to a chief who gathers and governs them, much like the branches of the same trunk.
H4294J.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of cutting, separation. A stick is first a piece of wood cut from the trunk — hence the natural link with the branch. The word also designates a rod of command, hence its use to speak of a tribe: a human group governed by a chief who holds the rod of power, as Moses held his marvelous rod.
H4294J.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the provided passages, all in the prophets. Two usages refer to the concrete stick (Isaiah) and two to the vine branch (Ezekiel). Ezekiel uses it in a poetic allegory: the vine symbolizes a royal house of Israel, its branches are its princely lineages, and their destruction prophesies the collapse of this power. The word translates the image of a living structure that divides and spreads, always from a single source.
H4294J.portee: This word shows how the Bible envisions community: like a unique vine that bears several branches, an original people that divides into tribes and families. It reminds the believer that he is never isolated but always part of a whole, a common history. It is also a lesson in humility: the largest branches can be broken and withered (Ezekiel 19:12), which invites one not to trust in one's own strength.

sens: Rigid and elongated object, usually made of wood, held in the hand
Support or means of sustenance, that which sustains life
H4294K.detail:
1. In the literal sense, a bâton is a solid and elongated object, such as a walking stick or a rod (for example, the rod of the shepherd who tended his flocks). It is an instrument that can be wielded or symbolizes authority.
2. In the figurative sense, the "bâton of bread" means the means of sustenance, that which allows one to live and be nourished. The expression "to break the bâton of bread" means to remove food, to send famine: "I will break the bâton of bread in Jerusalem" (Ezekiel 4:16). It is a powerful image of divine judgment that deprives a people of food as punishment for their unfaithfulness.
H4294K.origine: The Hebrew word מַטֶּה (matteh) comes from a root that expresses the idea of taking, holding. The bâton is primarily what one holds in hand, hence its evolution towards the meanings of "support" and "authority." In the Old Testament, the bâton is often the attribute of one who leads or supports (the shepherd with his bâton, the leader with his rod). The metaphor of the "bâton of bread" applies this image of support to food itself.
H4294K.emploi: The word appears 5 times in these passages, all from the section of Leviticus and the prophecies of Ezekiel regarding punishments. In all cases, it is used in the expression "to break the bâton of bread," which describes a famine sent by God in judgment for unfaithfulness. Leviticus 26:26 announces this punishment to the people who transgress the covenant; Ezekiel 4:16, 5:16, and 14:13 reiterate this same threat for Jerusalem and for other nations that sin. The meaning remains constant: the bâton of bread is not a physical object, but the resource that sustains life, and "to break it" means to create scarcity and famine.
H4294K.portee: The expression "to break the bâton of bread" reveals an important truth for the believer: food and life are not guaranteed, but depend on God and our obedience to His covenant. God uses famine as a sign of His judgment on sin and unfaithfulness, but also as a call to repentance. For the reader, this reminds us that material abundance is a gift from God, never an acquired right.

sens: The lower part of a thing, that which is below
The state of one who is submissive, inferior in rank or condition
The place where the dead dwell
The lower region of heaven
H4295.detail:
1. The lower part of a thing, that which is below: this word simply designates what is at the bottom, the base or underside of an object. In the descriptions of the Tabernacle, it refers to the boards "doubled from the bottom" (Exodus 26:24), meaning reinforced at their lower part.
2. The state of one who is submissive, inferior in rank or condition: "bas" describes a lowered social or moral position. When the Lord says to Israel, "you will never be in the bas" (Deuteronomy 28:13), He promises that the people will not be enslaved or dominated by other nations if they obey.
3. The place where the dead dwell: the "bas" can refer to the abode of the dead, the place of destruction. The wise "turns away from the abode of the dead which is below" (Proverbs 15:24), thus fleeing spiritual death.
4. The lower region of heaven: the word also evokes what extends beneath the firmament, the visible foundations of the created world (Jeremiah 31:37).
H4295.origine: This word comes from a root that means "to be low, to humble oneself." It is related to the feeling of what is inferior, humble, or degraded. The family of this word includes terms related to lowness, humiliation, inferiority. The basic image is always spatial: what is below in relation to what is above.
H4295.emploi: This word appears 18 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical and wisdom books. In Exodus and Chronicles, it describes material realities: the foundations or lower part of the structures of the Tabernacle (Exodus 26:24, 36:29). In the prophetic oracles, it takes on a more symbolic meaning: the position of weakness or servitude (Deuteronomy 28:13, 28:43), or the place of death and destruction (Proverbs 15:24). The cosmic usage appears when speaking of the "foundations of the earth below" to express the limits of the created world (Jeremiah 31:37).
H4295.portee: This word reminds the believer that the position "below" — whether physical, social, or spiritual — is never definitive. The Lord can lift up the one who is low and bring down the one who is exalted. It also invites us not to seek wisdom in the "below," the abode of the dead, but to look upward and toward the life that comes from God.

sens: Furniture intended for rest and sleep
The corpse of a deceased person, coffin or stretcher
H4296.detail:
1. The lit is primarily the piece of furniture on which one rests and sleeps: it is a place of intimacy and vulnerability. When Jacob is old, he bows "on the edge of his lit" (Genesis 47:31), marking the weight of years. The prophet Elisha places the dead child "on the lit of the man of God" (2 Kings 4:21), a gesture of tenderness before the resurrection. The lit can also be a place of illness and weakness: King Ahaziah, afflicted, receives the divine sentence: "You will not come down from the lit on which you have gone up, for you will die" (2 Kings 1:4).
2. By extension, the word designates the funeral bed, the coffin, or the stretcher that carries the dead. When Abner is killed, "King David walked behind the coffin" (2 Samuel 3:31), showing honor to the deceased. This meaning is less frequent but expresses the final rest of the body.
H4296.origine: The Hebrew word מִטָּה (mittah) is ancient and stable. It simply designates the lit as an object. Its basic image is that of a surface where one lies down. The word does not have a large morphological family in Hebrew, but its usage covers both daily rest and funeral rest, two forms of "stretching out the body."
H4296.emploi: The word mittah appears 29 times in the Old Testament. It is used in accounts of everyday life (sleeping, illness), where it often evokes a moment of vulnerability: Jacob dying on his lit (Genesis 48:2, 49:33), Elisha lying in the room of a kind woman (2 Kings 4:10). It also appears in descriptions of the temple and royal luxury, as in the account of Vashti (Esther 1:6) or that of Ezekiel (Ezekiel 23:41). The lit is also the place of carnal desire and excessive comfort (Amos 6:4 speaks of those "who are at ease on their lits"). In a funeral context, the term carries symbolic weight: it is on the lit that the dead rests before being taken to burial (2 Samuel 3:31).
H4296.portee: The lit reminds the reader that they are corporeal, that they need rest, and that they are mortal. The Bible does not despise the rest of the body, but invites us not to cling to it in a carnal way. The lit is also the place of intimacy with God: it is lying on his lit that Jacob sees the ladder to heaven in a dream. For the Christian, the word invites a proper relationship with rest, illness, and death.

sens: Distortion or deformation of what is right
Absence of justice, action contrary to the law
Wickedness, perversity in conduct
H4297.detail:
1. The word denotes a distortion or deformation of what should be right and just. It is the image of something twisted, bent, perverted. In Ezekiel 9:9, the iniquity of Israel and Judah is described as filling the land, alongside murders: it is a systematic malice, an injustice rooted in the people.
2. More broadly, it refers to the absence of justice and violation of the law in relationships between people or before God. This injustice reflects a perversion of the order that God has established, a refusal of righteousness and fairness.
H4297.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to turn," "to divert," "to pervert." It carries the image of something that has been bent or deviated from its natural course. This family of words expresses the idea of twisting or perversion, applied here to human actions and attitudes that stray from divine justice.
H4297.emploi: This word appears only once in the biblical text (Ezekiel 9:9). In this passage from the prophet Ezekiel, iniquity is associated with murders as one of the great sins that fill Jerusalem and the land of Judah. It appears in a vision of divine judgment, where God shows Ezekiel the extent of moral corruption before sending His punishment. Injustice here is a serious moral crime, a systematic violation of divine justice.
H4297.portee: This word reminds us that injustice is not merely a weakness or a temporary imperfection: it is a perversion, a voluntary or persistent diversion from what is just. For the Christian, this highlights the seriousness of the sin of injustice and the importance of actively seeking righteousness and fairness in one's relationships and actions, by imitating God's justice.

sens: Wide extension of open wings
Expansion that invades or overflows
Visible and imposing manifestation of a force
H4298.detail: 1. The deployment refers to the action of extending or unfolding, particularly the wings of a bird that open wide. It is the image of a majestic wingspan that spreads out in space (Isaiah 8:8 speaks of the deployment of an eagle's wings). 2. By extension, it is the rapid expansion of a force that occupies space, overflowing and invading: the image remains that of a wing that extends over an entire region and covers it (Isaiah 8:8 shows this: the enemy that "overflows" is described by this word of "deployment" that fills the whole land). 3. Therefore, it is a visible, impressive manifestation that imposes itself to the eye — something that cannot go unnoticed.
H4298.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to extend" or "to open." It evokes the natural image of wings that unfold. The same root produces other words concerning extension or deployment.
H4298.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 8:8. There, the prophet describes the invasion of the kingdom of Assyria against Judah using the image of an eagle: its wings extend and cover the land of Emmanuel. The context is one of an overwhelming threat that extends irresistibly, covering everything in its path.
H4298.portee: This word reminds us that God is in control of history, even when human powers seem to deploy their force overwhelmingly. Isaiah speaks of the deployment of the enemy's wings, but just before (verses 7-8), he established that God is with Judah. The imposing deployment of empires contrasts with the protection that God promises to His people.

sens: Thread obtained by spinning, wound on itself
Work of spinning, finished product ready for use
H4299.detail:
1. The word denotes the thread that spinners create by twisting and winding textile fibers (wool, linen) on a spindle or distaff. It is the concrete product of spinning, before it is woven. In Exodus 35:25, skilled women produce this "work" spun in different colors — blue, purple, scarlet — which will be used for the construction of the tabernacle.
2. The word can also more broadly refer to the finished work of spinning, the fruit of the manual skill of spinners: not only the thread itself but the work, the production they bring for the service of God.
H4299.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the action of twisting, of twirling. It is related to the idea of transforming raw fibers into continuous and strong thread through a repetitive and skilled gesture — a very concrete image of ancient artisanal work.
H4299.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 35:25. It is mentioned in the context of the voluntary gifts of Israelite women for the construction of the tabernacle. The women bring not only thread of different colors (blue, purple, scarlet) but also fine linen: all these spun materials are essential for the embroidery and decoration of the priest's garments and the holy enclosure.
H4299.portee: This verse honors the humble and skillful work of women in the service of God. Their delicate spinning is not just a simple domestic task: it is a valuable contribution to worship, an offering of their hands and intelligence. It reminds the reader that any well-done work, however humble, becomes sacred when it serves the house of God and His people.
